t: Ten Things to Understand About Research and Reading Instruction
q: Research answers specific research questions and is used to validate specific research hypotheses. It is a snapshot taken of a small slice of reality, set in the context of a specific time and place, with specific conditions, participants, and methodology.
A single study can support a point, but it does not prove a point. When looking at research, you can’t look at a single study to determine anything conclusively.

For example, to conclude that structured literacy is more effective than balanced literacy instruction, you’d want the conclusion to be based on peer-reviewed research comparing two groups, one using structured literacy and the other using balanced literacy. And the groups must be equivalent in terms of demographics and conditions.

How are teacher supposed to know what research-based reading instruction is or to make research-based decisions if they are denied access to research? How are they supposed to know what a body of research says about something if they are not provided access to a body of research?

q: This has probably happened for one of three reasons. Firstly, the student has focused on the wrong thing, such as revising content which does not appear on a test. Secondly, their approach is inefficient, meaning the time spent has little impact on their knowledge and skill.

The motivational curve is hill-shaped in that the optimal strategy is to tell students enough for them to believe that their efforts can change the outcome, but not so much as to reassure them that they already know enough.

t: An Ethic of Basic Probity
q: Why do people, even those who occupy the top rungs of society’s key institutions, lie so much today? Because it works. Because it’s rewarded.
Societies that wish to overcome the toxic effects of rampant dishonesty have to establish systems that reward telling the truth and punish lying.

And the answer, to be clear, is not to say that the bad guys are so vicious and opportunistic that we need to beat them by any means necessary! It’s to try to rebuild an ethic of basic probity, honesty, and factual accuracy from the ground up.

Multitudinous cultural changes have undermined the structural underpinnings of a culture of honesty. That’s not to say everyone was honest in the past - far from it - but there was an era in which honesty was a social norm, and in which being found a liar might well suffer significant consequences.

I would say that while Elizabeth Holmes style whoppers are a problem in our society, equally or more seriously as bad is the extreme go-along-to-get-along mentality that has been adopted by so many of our institutional leaders.

t: Admissions as a compression algorithm
q: Start with what an admissions office actually is. It is a device for compressing three or four years of a human being into something a reader can evaluate in eight minutes. GPA is lossy compression of coursework.

Almost everything in an application is an assertion about the student rather than an artifact by the student. The transcript asserts that learning happened. The rec asserts character.

t: Louise Cowan's Speech on Teachers - Part I
q: Teachers are instructing the young then not primarily to enable their charges to succeed in life but to preserve and extend the heritage of a civilization—to pass on what is culturally valuable.
Families and neighborhoods are not schools, which have a unique intent and purpose—the formation of citizens who are knowledgeable enough—and wise enough—to govern themselves.

We have tended to make the teaching process sound more like behavioral instruction (something like the training of young animals) than the drawing out of noble aspects in rational and imaginative beings.
We’ve taken away the elevating metaphors from our education—those bundles of symbolic content that have a kind of magical power to reveal a nobility that would otherwise remain hidden.

A teacher is not really needed for the mastery of facts and skills; to gain this sort of information something simply has to capture student attention long enough for bits of data to sink in—or for practice to make perfect.

For facts are mere information, and skills are mere habits of behavior, and neither is necessarily related to principles and virtues needing to be instilled in our young if our democracy is to survive.
Sometime back in the 20th century, which now seems like another epoch completely, we started substituting the word “value” for the older word “virtue.
x: A teacher, she says, has the twofold task of forming the young for their own sake and for society's, preserving and extending the heritage of a civilization.
In this speech for a Learning Center dedication, curated from the Cowan Archive, Louise Cowan distinguishes teachers from other mentors such as parents and coaches.
She criticizes a modern philosophy that treats teaching as behavioral training, strips out elevating metaphors and reduces education to facts, skills and incessant testing.
Modern education has become literal, fact- and skill-centered and test-driven, losing the elevating metaphors that reveal nobility.
Machines can deliver information and skills, but not the principles and virtues a democracy needs.

t: Lead by Compass, Not Calendar
q: We must orient ourselves by what doesn’t expire or shift. If plans and quarterly goals must shift before we reach them, it feels like the present is always shrinking.

When conditions move fast, the work shifts from executing a schedule to recognizing when the moment is right. That’s a different leadership capacity, closer to discernment than planning.
As a CEO, and across the leaders I work with, I have seen what happens when a chapter is never closed: forces of inertia keep pulling the organization back.
The present is the only place we can act. You know this. It is not a mantra. It is true.
We can no longer mark time by where we planned to be. We have to mark it by who we are and where we find ourselves, right now.

t: I'm not doing 996.
q: There’s a big difference between working hard with working all the time.

t: How Mature Is Your Team?
q: Most notably, mature teams are willing to talk about their mistakes. In fact, in a study of hospital units, mature teams reported more medical errors, not fewer.

t: Where Does School Segregation Come From?

Between-district segregation is a different problem. Imagine a predominantly white suburban district bordering a predominantly Black urban district.

That’s because the biggest component of racial economic segregation, by far, is between districts. Think of these as housing and district boundary issues, and they contribute 59% of the total.
In fact, the Century Foundation found that between-district differences accounted for 76% of racial segregation in the Northeast, compared with just 41% in the South.

So if policymakers want to address the largest source of segregation, especially in the Northeast and the Midwest, they would need to pursue things like open enrollment, regional magnet schools, changes to district boundaries, or housing policies that allow more families to live in high-opportunity neighborhoods.

t: What If Human Flourishing Became Part of the Measure?
q: We measure revenue, productivity, growth, utilization, efficiency, return on investment, test scores, patient volume, housing units, voter turnout, program participation, and countless other things. Many of those measures are important.
But somewhere along the way, I wonder whether we have allowed the measurement to become the outcome.
A structure can become more efficient while making life worse for the people inside it. An organization can grow while exhausting the people who make that growth possible.

t: The Thing Keeping Me Safe Was the Thing I Should Have Feared
q: The fear that keeps you where you are does not arrive as fear. It arrives as good judgment.

My value was real, but it was circumstantial. It could be spent, managed, and emailed about on a Sunday, and the moment the deal was signed, it would reset to whatever the next unfinished thing required of me.
It came disguised as every value I respect. Pragmatism. Patience. Providing for my family.

It feels identical, in the body, to the fear that warns you off a genuine cliff. Same churn, same tightening, same airtight case for not moving. One is protecting your life. The other is protecting your cage.
What changed was not the fear. It was how I read it. I stopped treating it as a verdict and started treating it as information to interpret.
The strangest part is that frightening and free turn out to be the same feeling from the inside. The drop in your stomach when you step off the ladder is almost identical to the drop of falling.
I used to be afraid of not climbing high enough. That fear is gone. What scares me now is reaching eighty and not being able to say, in one clear sentence, how my life made something better.

q: The causes of reading difficulty are complex and varied, but reading gaps are primarily gaps in phonics, knowledge and practice, and the gaps compound over time.

Within the first year of school, large differences in reading practice can emerge: children who experience greater difficulty when breaking the sound-spelling code will be exposed to less text than their peers because they are still mastering the knowledge needed to read longer books.

Less word-reading practice delays the development of fast, automatic word recognition, which places greater demands on working memory and reduces capacity to understand, and make meaning from, what’s being read.

A Nagy and Anderson 1984 study, cited here, estimates that the least motivated readers in middle school might read 100,000 words a year, while the most motivated might read 10,000,000. This is a staggering gap!
Though we may not be able to identify why a student’s reading difficulties began, we can identify the gaps and do something about them.

a decoding intervention can address an important foundational gap but it cannot, on its own, make up for years of reduced reading experience or close the resulting gaps in vocabulary, general knowledge, syntactic knowledge and reading fluency.

Because children who struggle with the code meet less text, they get less word-reading practice, which delays automatic word recognition, burdens working memory and drives avoidance of reading.

t: How to Recognize When You Have Stopped Growing
q: The trouble is that stagnation rarely announces itself. It arrives dressed as mastery, wearing the clothes of competence and walking with ease.

When pushback fades, many leaders conclude they have earned the trust of others. The less flattering explanation is that they have become too expensive to disagree with.

t: Did you choose your career or just the next job?

t: A case against the “Education Revolution”
q: Revolutionising” education because of AI is like burning down your house because you need new carpet.
Much of what matters most in education hasn’t changed at all.

Technological change is not additive; it is ecological... A new medium does not add something; it changes everything. In the year 1500, after the printing press was invented, you did not have old Europe plus the printing press. You had a different Europe.
The purpose of education. Schools are still producing people, not producing work. The aim of a school was never the essay; it was the formation of the student writing it.
Attention is finite, memory is the residue of thought, and the brain still takes the easy path whenever it’s offered. AI didn’t create that tendency. It just made the easy path shorter.
People were more willing to support change when leaders also articulated what would stay the same. And the effect was strongest when uncertainty was highest.
When all we talk about is revolution, our staff hear that everything they value is up for grabs, and they can often dig in and resist change.
Being clear about what isn’t changing is less about avoiding change and more about managing change wisely.

t: What Are the "Look Fors" in Secondary Literacy Programs?
q: Reading comprehension is not a skill per se. Proficient comprehension depends upon understanding how different texts work, knowledge of the world, competence with language, and so on.

My uncertainty as to potency of such literature in terms of improving reading achievement should not be interpreted as an opposition to including texts that reflect a wide range of cultural diversity. Nothing could be further from the truth.

English teachers have become quite adept at identifying worthwhile texts (in terms of literary merit, cultural value, thematic relevance, etc.) that are relatively easy for their students to read. t: The Loud Liker Theory
q: The collision of these two scientific findings is painful. In effect, you send less than you think, and you hear less than they send. Two people who like each other leave an interaction convinced the other one doesn’t.
In simple terms, our fear of rejection in social situations tempers our ability to convey social signals, and blinds our ability to recognize that tempering effect.

Across multiple, diverse contexts, researchers found that people systematically underestimate their conversation partner’s liking for them. Third party observers accurately estimated how much each party liked the other, but participants themselves were blind to it.
Researchers believe it’s driven by our own self-critical internal monologue, paired with a natural egocentric bias that overemphasizes our own flaws.
If I admire something someone did, I send them a message to let them know. Big or small, it doesn’t matter.

t: The Definition of Psychological Safety
q: Psychological safety is defined asthe belief, in a group, that we are safe to take interpersonal risks. It’s the belief that we are able to speak up with ideas, questions, concerns and mistakes, and that we won’t suffer negative social or professional consequences as a result.
A clear definition acts like a compass pointing to True North, without which we could be heading in different directions.
Terms often suffer from “epistemic drift” – a passive drift away from their intended meaning.

Psychological safety, for example, addresses only interpersonal risks, not physical, business, health or other risks. When psychological safety is mistakenly framed as permitting business or safety risks, it misleads people.

Overly simplistic definitions, like “Psychological safety is the ability to speak up without fear,” reduce the concept to just “speaking up” and overlook the complexities of social interactions and the need to create an environment where people can communicate and share in different ways.

Conversely, overly broad definitions may suggest psychological safety is about always feeling comfortable, having no accountability, or being your “authentic self”. These frame psychological safety as synonymous with comfort – which it is absolutely not.
Our shared commitment to rigour, clarity, and continual learning and growth in this area is what will help keep psychological safety from drifting into just another meaningless leadership fad.
x: Tom Geraghty explains why his team opens every talk and workshop by restating the working definition of psychological safety: the belief, in a group, that it is safe to take interpersonal risks.
Shared definitions prevent conversations and debates from failing simply because participants use the same term differently.

Definitions also set boundaries, so psychological safety covers interpersonal risk and not physical, business or health risk.

t: Rethinking the Foundation Subjects
q: The trap to avoid is planning by the number of lessons available. It’s tempting. You’d have all that content and only 6-8 weeks (lessons usually) to fit in the most important stuff. But this will always lead to packing in too much.

The national curriculum subject content is not enough to teach from. Subject experts need to specific the exact substantive knowledge that we want children to learn, the associated vocabulary, the concepts that children should develop (and how they’ll develop over time) and the disciplinary knowledge too.

The sequence of learning should not be bound by arbitrary time limits. It will take as long as it takes for children to learn it and this is important because it is part of whole, a sequence of learning that affects the whole school and not just one year group.
Classic conveyor belt education; the next lesson and the next unit of work comes along regardless of what children have learned.

The important question for teachers is: ‘What do you do when children haven’t understood?’ We can’t just move on. We need wiggle room in units of work to spend longer (or shorter) on different ideas so that it is truly responsive to what children know and understand.
No need to track teacher assessments for foundation subjects. We’d simply be putting information into a spreadsheet that then spits out the same information. Pointless.
The importance of assessment in the foundation subjects is that of formative assessment. And formative assessment is only useful if we actually do something with the the information.

t: Play: The Glue That Connects Us
q: We still had a nice vacation that summer, but something had changed; the play had stopped. Now, almost fifty years later, I can see how easily we can begin to drift apart when we stop making time to play together.
When you work, work with focus, diligence and grit, but taking time to play not only recharges the battery, it connects team members and fosters creativity.
Play isn’t just a reward we earn after the work is finished, because let’s face it – if you’re ambitious, the work is never finished.
So, this week, I encourage you to make room for a little more fun. Put down the phone, close the laptop, and invite your wife and kids to do something simply because it’s enjoyable.
Over 2,300 years ago, Aristotle recognized that a good life requires more than hard work, and that living well requires learning how to enjoy worthwhile activities, not simply how to be productive.

But all work and no play is a strategy that most often backfires, because good family memories aren’t made when you’re out there achieving your goals. They’re made when we put the work aside and simply enjoy being together.

Not every moment needs to be turned into a teaching opportunity and you certainly don’t need to make everything productive. Sometimes, the best thing you can do for your family is simply enjoy being together.
Your kids won’t remember everything you did for them, but they’ll remember how it felt to be with you.

t: Most Business Problems Are First and Foremost People Problems
q: Most business problems are, at their root, people problems. Missed forecasts, stalled initiatives, or failed integrations look like a matter of weak execution, systems, or process, but look closer and you will find people making choices that make sense to them.
Sound strategies routinely collapse in execution because the people asked to carry them out do not believe in them, do not understand them, or see them as a threat.
Reorganizations that look clean on an org chart unravel because each team member judges the change by what it does to their own standing, workload, or future.
People also act on their perception of reality, not on the reality itself. Hand the same budget overrun to three executives and you will get three different problems.
The gap is rarely about the facts. It is almost always about what each person wants, fears, and believes is at stake.
Good leaders tailor their approach, offering data to those who need proof, reassurance to those who feel threatened, and a real voice to those whose commitment will make or break the result.
Leaders who first understand who they are dealing with will find the right solution easier to identify, build support for, and execute.

t: Blame
q: It’s a common fallacy that psychological safety means having a “blameless” culture. Just like so many misconceptions around psychological safety, that’s not actually the case.
Blame can be considered “accountability without context“, so a powerful way to address blame is to actively and explicitly consider context.
If we jump to blame, we can easily miss all this nuance and any opportunities to better understand and learn from the multitude of compounding factors.
Instead of fostering learning, this may instead foster resentment and damage confidence in someone’s capability or self-worth.
What’s more, publicly-imposed blame is likely to teach others to hide their mistakes, suppress their concerns, and “keep their head down” lest they suffer the same public humiliation.
A far more constructive and utilitarian approach is to treat errors, mistakes and violations as sources of valuable information about the system.

By recognising our own inherent blametropism – our innate instinct to apportion blame – and becoming blame-aware instead of (maybe naively) attempting to be entirely blameless or blame-free, we can check in with ourselves and others to help determine whether we’re blaming because it’ll make us feel better, or whether it’s actually a constructive thing to do.

t: You Must Cling to Your College Friends
q: Friendship is the real solution to the loneliness epidemic that’s sending many in our society down a dark life path.

Outside of online dating, the best way to meet potential partners is through friends. Your friends are able to introduce you to their coworkers, their neighbors, their cousins, and other new people they meet.

q: Leaders who use this expression frequently tell others that they are open to competing views and perspectives. Pound for pound, this is one of the most powerful expressions in a leader’s repertoire.

Any questions?” and “Does everyone agree?” invite people to confirm what the leader already believes, and most people take the invitation. “What am I missing?” assumes the leader’s view is incomplete and invites people to fill in the gap.
But the expression only works if the leader means it. Team members watch closely to see what happens after someone offers a missing piece.
The best leaders treat every answer as a gift. They thank the person, ask a follow-up question, and when the input changes their thinking, they say so out loud.
Over time, the habit compounds in its effect. Leaders hear about problems while there is still time to fix them.
Team members learn that their judgment, and not just their agreement, is wanted. And leaders model the confidence that does not depend on being right.

t: The Work Beneath the Work
q: One of the reasons we tend towards burnout this time of year is that there's a work beneath our work.

Want to burn yourself out? Submit yourself to the ceaseless striving that such work beneath the work tyrannically calls us to.
Teaching — the real work — is wholly other-centered, totally focused on creating something new in someone else.
Teaching's real work turns the teacher into a tool for one of humanity's oldest magics — the passing on of knowledge, skills, and wisdom from one generation to the next.
The teachers who flourish for the duration — who reach the true mark of teaching greatness, which is longevity — continually bring themselves back to what the real work is.

t: The Courage to Look Like the Bad Guy
q: One of the most difficult forms of discipline to practice is choosing not to shield someone from the consequences of their actions.
If you shield people from consequences over and over again, they will continue to act foolishly. It can actually embolden them to become more reckless.
Sometimes one of the most unloving things ever done to someone is shielding him from the consequences of his actions.
My dad drew a line in the sand and maintained it, and that helped me grow up.
There are absolutely times to overlook things. You certainly don’t want to make things bigger than they are, and there’s a big difference between simple mistakes and deliberate foolishness.
We must cultivate a gracious attitude that loves people enough to disappoint them, even when that means letting them take a hard landing without cushioning the fall.

Whether it’s letting your child repeat a grade, letting someone get fired from a job, or excommunicating an unrepentant church member, you must have the courage to look like the bad guy and not look the other way.

t: The Brain Doesn't Care How Clear Your Explanation Was
q: The acid in your stomach is strong enough to dissolve metal. So why does it not dissolve you? Did you feel that? Something shifted. Your brain leaned in. You needed the answer.
Clear explanations matter slowly became clear explanation = learning. And children have been paying the cost ever since.

Children don’t walk into our classrooms waiting for explanations. They walk in with their own explanations. Mental models about how the world works built from everything they’ve seen, heard, and experienced.

The brain actively protects its current understanding. Changing it takes real mental effort. So the brain does not absorb new information because it was explained clearly. It absorbs information when it has a reason to.
So the design question is not just: How do I explain this clearly? It’s: How do I make the learner need the explanation before it arrives?
Before you explain, students need to already be thinking, wondering, predicting, or trying to resolve something. Explanations land differently when the brain is already searching for an answer.
Why it works: predictions make the brain commit before the explanation arrives. Once you’ve committed to an answer, you care whether you were right.

t: The Blank Brain Problem: What the Loss of Thinking is Costing Our Students
q: AI can improve the work while quietly weakening the thinker—especially when it answers before we have made a first attempt.

The tool can fill the blank page, but it cannot automatically fill the mind of the person who submitted the prompt. A student can receive a complete paragraph without developing the knowledge needed to write one.

If young people routinely outsource the first attempt, they may miss the experiences that make thinking possible: recalling what they know, tolerating uncertainty, testing an idea, discovering it doesn't work, and trying again.
Learning is different because the internal change matters more than the external product. Effort isn't always an obstacle between the learner and the lesson. Sometimes the effort is the lesson.
The question is not, “Can AI make this easier?” It almost always can. The better question is, “What kind of effort will disappear if it does?

The lesson is not that AI has no place in learning. The design and sequence of help matter. A tool that supplies the answer can raise immediate performance while reducing the learning needed for later independence.
The most practical rule I have arrived at is simple: when the process is supposed to develop you, do not give AI the first move.
Use AI early when the process is expendable. Use it later—and more carefully—when the process is developmental. Let it remove the work that steals time from thinking, not the work that is thinking.

t: School Calendars Are a Choice
q: Many large districts in the D.C. area and around the country have stretched their school calendars across more days of the year, even as students receive the same amount of instruction. The difference is more days off scattered throughout the year for religious holidays, teacher professional development, and other breaks.
I support school leaders to reflect on how their policies and decisions reflect their values, and that even a default is a choice.

You mentioned having a lot of Mondays and Fridays off, but even worse are random Tuesdays and Thursdays or half-day Wednesdays, which are not aligned to federal holidays and not aligned to any normal adult schedules.
It can mean forgoing wages or using vacation days, and it’s essentially a financial tax on parents, not to mention the mental load of having to keep track of it all.

In most school districts, half days count for a full day of instruction toward the state’s 180-day mandate. So it’s a way for districts to squeeze in things that they think are important, like professional development for teachers, and still count it as a full day of school, even when kids are not getting a full day of instruction.
When we don’t plan, what ends up happening is that instruction is not made up in any meaningful way. Too many snow days can put kids and teachers behind.

t: How Sport Built My Leadership Before I Knew I Was Leading
q: Sport, whether playing or coaching, has a way of exposing your weaknesses. As a young and naïve coach, I made plenty of mistakes — the kind I now look back on and cringe.
But more importantly, that coach invested time in me. He saw something I didn’t yet see in myself — and in many ways, set me on the path towards coaching, mentoring and teaching.
Every loss felt personal. Every result felt like a judgement. My dad would often say, “Why are you taking this so much to heart?
I moved away from control and towards trust. From outcomes to process. From blame to ownership.
If a player made a mistake trying to do what I had asked, I took responsibility. Not them. I wanted players to feel safe to take risks.
If there’s improvement, then progress has been made. And if progress has been made, then you’re doing your job.
Because leadership — real leadership — isn’t something you switch on. It’s something that’s built, often long before you realise you’re leading at all.
x: Paul Robinson, a PE teacher and coach, traces how playing and coaching football shaped his approach to leadership.
He begins with a trial where a coach made him captain within minutes, an early act of trust that set him on a path toward coaching and teaching.
Sport exposes weakness, and the author’s early habits of shouting, seeking validation and taking results personally are presented as a baseline from which to grow.

t: How "Free Money" Breeds Shadow IT
q: In Medium and Large Companies a political game determines how the organization operates and how things actually get done.
These internal recharges are how the real game is played. It is where decision-makers and department heads find creative ways to let initiatives fly under the radar when they lack a dedicated budget.
The problem begins when that “project” becomes a multi-year endeavor with ongoing efforts. Operational costs are masked as “projects”, and no internal recharge really happens.
This is one of the ways Shadow IT is born: when other departments manage to hire IT skills to produce software that is not under IT governance.

A lack of internal recharges shows a lack of structure and control over how money is spent inside the company. Assigning budget lines with multi-year renewals on a perpetual basis is not project management. It is a lack of management altogether.
If someone is doing software for “free”, they will eventually need the capabilities of an IT department for maintenance and support.
If your castle is well maintained, it is natural to demand the same level of rigor from other departments.

t: Homer, Teacher of Us All
q: Homer, it seems to me, isn’t at all convinced that history has an intelligible pattern. I don’t mean that he actively disbelieves in such a pattern, which would align him with the postmoderns; I simply don’t think the question would ever have occurred to him.

Virgil’s pattern is political and his use of the past rhetorical, almost propagandistic. He’s a marvelous poet, but his poem is suffused throughout with a layer of political significance lacking in Homer.
That’s how some critics nowadays read everything, and it spoils the reading experience — especially because the political key is always presumed to be revolutionary.
Homer immortalized this full, contradictory vision of life as a common treasury from which all later Western thinkers have plundered only some things as worth keeping.
Whether we like it or not, even whether we admit it or not, we all suffer from the postmodern problem.

The political myths of other epics universalize given answers to the problem of life and death, but Homer refuses to answer: he’s content simply to show us men wrestling with the question — and therefore to show us ourselves.
Homer, therefore, is an indispensable first teacher for postmodern students seeking to fulfill the Delphic command to “know thyself.

Lewis's distinction between primary and secondary epic, he contrasts Virgil, whose pattern of history is political and almost propagandistic, with Homer, who is free of political and philosophical partisanship.

Homer accepts war and peace, love and hatred, life and death without excluding anything for the sake of an idea or allegiance, which is why later Western thinkers draw on him.

t: From Disengaged to Selective: The Profiles of Young Adult Daters
q: Specifically, we found that less than a third of young adults in the prime serious dating years (ages 22-35)—who expect to marry in the future—are dating at least once a month.
Simply put, it is not very helpful to see all young adults through a single statistic of central tendency.
Interestingly, the three groups are equally dissatisfied with their dating options (although their “meh” feelings might come from different experiences).
Selective Daters—the other low-frequency-dating group, and the largest group overall—have much higher confidence in their dating skills.
Young adults who are dating the most do so for social reasons and have fears of serious relationships and commitment, even though marriage is important and salient to them.
This group, it seems, needs more help finding dating partners who match their serious orientation to dating. They need dating pathways more than dating education.

Using the 2025 National Dating Landscape Survey, they argue that a single statistic hides diversity and identify three dater profiles.

The dating recession is not uniform: low-frequency dating hides two very different groups, the unprepared and the selective.
Active daters date for social reasons and fear commitment, partly because of painful past breakups, so they need resilience and help examining their fears.
Selective daters are confident and serious and appear to need dating pathways that match their intent more than dating education.

t: From Blank Page to Written Argument
q: But writing is not only a way to demonstrate learning. It is also a way to develop learning.

A few minutes of low-stakes writing each day helps students collect ideas, rehearse language, and discover what they think. By essay day, they have a trail of words behind them, so are not beginning with nothing.
Structured peer conversation gives students a rehearsal space for writing. Then when they face the blank page, the words are not entirely new. They have already spoken some of them aloud.
Students must first put their own thinking into words and then use those words to build knowledge with others.
To speak from another perspective, students must reach for different claims, evidence, and vocabulary.

An outline can organize ideas, but it cannot supply language students have never practiced using. A graphic organizer can hold evidence, but it cannot replace the intellectual work of discussing what that evidence means.
Collaborative writing and structured talk do not lower expectations for independent work. They prepare students to meet those expectations.
x: Stephany Anderson, a secondary English teacher, starts from the scene of ninth graders staring at a blank page on essay day even after outlining and analysing sample essays.
Writing is a way to develop learning as well as to demonstrate it, so students need regular low-stakes writing before any graded essay.
Her answer is writing to learn and talking to learn: low-stakes journaling before the assessment and structured peer conversation as a rehearsal space for academic language.
She reframes the problem from why students will not write to how teachers help them find the words and get them onto the page.

t: Educators Should Embrace the ‘Science of Math.’ Here’s Why h-heres-why/2026/10
q: Both are highly cumulative, and early skills strongly predict later ones. If you cannot link letters to sounds, you will struggle to become a fluent reader.
There is a lot of research on how children learn about numbers and math. But in my experience, too little of it reaches teacher training and professional development.
Math lacks such a straightforward sequence. It is multifaceted, and the learning sequence for algebra differs from geometry.

Traditionalists tend to emphasize teaching the standard algorithm, while progressives usually argue that children should be taught multiple strategies and develop their own conceptual understanding. My take is that we should think about math instruction developmentally.

Kirschner also argued that minimally guided instructional approaches—like discovery learning and problem-based instruction—are less effective for most novices because those students don’t yet have enough knowledge stored in memory, so they need external guidance.
Once they’ve reached a high level of accuracy, timed activities help them consolidate their math facts into long-term memory, so they can retrieve them later when solving more advanced problems.

The science of math is meant to help teachers and school leaders become more effective at educating students. Researchers can tell you what tends to work. But teachers are the only ones who can figure out what that means in your school.

t: Beyond the Phonics Wars: Why Zig Engelmann Was Always Building Knowledge
q: This critique is not just incomplete—it fundamentally misapprehends what Zig Engelmann spent his life creating.

Critics often confuse the content of a lesson with the pedagogy used to deliver it. They assume that because DI employs highly scripted, fast-paced, explicit sequences, it must be restricted to simple, rote mechanics.

Direct Instruction is a methodology for faultless communication—a system engineered to eliminate misinterpretation so that students learn complex concepts as efficiently as possible. There is zero logical reason why explicit, clear pedagogy cannot convey rich, challenging, and domain-specific knowledge.
Students acquire domain knowledge first, ensuring that when they encounter complex literary narratives, they have the requisite schema to extract meaning and apply high-level reasoning.

This curriculum does not merely teach syntax and mechanics; it builds a systematic framework for logical thinking. It teaches children how to construct arguments, analyze evidence, identify fallacies, draw valid inferences, and organize complex ideas.
Engelmann was not interested in creating passive readers who could merely bark at print. He was building thinkers.
Zig Engelmann never accepted those false choices. He recognized that to give every child access to rich content, deep knowledge, and rigorous logic, you cannot leave their learning to chance.
The explicit precision of DI isn't the opposite of knowledge building—it is its most powerful accelerator.

t: Authority Gets Compliance, Trust Gets Commitment
q: You may have the authority to direct your team’s actions, but that doesn’t mean you have earned their trust.
Trust is built slowly—but can be damaged surprisingly quickly. You can spend months establishing leadership credibility and weaken it with one poorly handled situation.
Your words said one thing. Your behavior taught something completely different. People usually trust the behavior. Not the statement.
Listen without interrupting or defending your decision. Then summarize what you heard before responding.
You may eventually need to explain your reasoning. But explanation before understanding can sound like justification.
The first step in rebuilding trust is often demonstrating that you understand why it was damaged.
Instead, identify the behavior that created the problem and replace it with a visible, repeatable action.
x: Trust becomes developmental when reflection turns into behavior, so ask a colleague what you do that builds or weakens confidence and pick one action for this week.
Rebuilding trust begins with showing you understand why it was damaged.
A quick trust test asks whether words and actions match, since people believe the behavior over the statement.
He gives a practical scenario in which a leader invites an opposing perspective on a work-allocation change, listens without defending, and summarizes before responding.

t: Are Your Customers Unhappy? Would You Know If They Were?
q: Most CEOs think they know how their customers feel. That is usually a comforting belief that isn’t quite true.
A big number is uncomfortable, but it tells you the news is getting through and you can do something about it. A zero should really worry you.
Most of the time, customers won’t tell you when you disappoint them. They just move on and engage less.
It’s not that the sales leader is hiding customer dissatisfaction on purpose. But when your boss’s bonus depends on the story being good, the story gets softer.
A customer can renew for two years out of inertia and be unhappy the whole time. A good Customer Success function reads between those lines.
No single function is equipped on its own to diagnose the issue and decide on the proper resolution. It requires the CEO’s 10,000-foot view.
Keep a running count of every time a customer was let down and review it monthly. If it’s suspiciously empty, be suspicious.
x: He uses it to argue that most CEOs only believe they know how customers feel, and that unless feedback machinery reaches them they live in a bubble.
A quarterly question to the leadership team, how many times did we hear about disappointing a customer, exposes whether bad news is reaching the top, and a zero should worry a CEO.
Customers rarely complain when disappointed; they disengage and later cite budget, so by the time it reaches the CEO as churn it is too late.
He explains why Customer Success should not report to sales: the sales leader is paid for bookings and momentum, so bad news gets softened and the function drifts toward account management.
Placing Customer Success under sales creates an incentive to soften bad news and turns the function into renewal and upsell management.
Because customer problems often span product, sales and pricing, only the CEO has the view to diagnose and resolve them.
Practical steps include measuring the Customer Success leader on retention and outcomes, keeping a running count of customer letdowns, and letting the team escalate without permission.

t: Are You Immune To Changing?
q: We all have a kind of emotional immune system that protects us from the anticipated potential negative effects of change. The job of your emotional immune system is to keep the status quo and protect you from the emotional dangers that might result from you making significant changes in your life.
Despite a stern warning—change or die—patients still could not change their diet and exercise habits.
Kegan and Lahey help people examine the competing commitments that may be in direct conflict with the goals they set.
Changing our behavior is surprisingly difficult because our core beliefs are often the result of deeply ingrained behaviors that arise from childhood emotional survival strategies.
He was not aware that he ultimately believed that leaders who delegated things were “lazy and selfish, and dumped their responsibilities on the people that worked under them.
No amount of teaching delegation skills (technical skills) was going to change David’s behavior.
The idea of experimenting is essential here because it’s easier to say you are experimenting than to put the pressure on yourself to immediately change your behavior and make it permanent right away.

Parker Houston summarizes Robert Kegan and Lisa Lahey's Immunity to Change, which distills 25 years of Harvard research into why leaders and organizations struggle to make changes they say they want.
People often cannot change because they hold competing commitments, like having a foot on the gas and the brake at the same time.
The CEO case shows that a goal such as delegating more can fail because it contradicts a core belief about what a real leader does.
A case study of a CEO who could not delegate shows that his goal clashed with a belief that delegating leaders are lazy and selfish, so delegation skills alone could never solve it.
Technical training cannot fix an adaptive challenge; the underlying belief must be reframed before skills can take hold.

t: AI, messy jobs, and the future of schooling
q: Whatever you think of AI’s potential upsides—and I believe they are significant—the most urgent questions around artificial intelligence in education have to do with minimizing harm.
Jobs that amount to a single routine task, or even a bundle of routine tasks, can and will be automated.

If, therefore, you spend a lot of time sitting in meetings, working toward decisions with colleagues and clients, selling to customers, or solving problems, then good news: Your job will be hard to automate!

But to use AI effectively—especially to spot errors or misjudgments—we need people who possess deep domain expertise. That means fully developing students’ cognitive capacities and helping them become experts in something.
Concerns about early career pipelines are real, legitimate, and hard to solve.
But if AI can do many of the junior-level tasks as well or better than junior workers, this model breaks down. It’s hard for firms to charge dearly for the labor of their junior employees.

Unless you think AIs are set to become very effective at teaching most students (which I do not, in no small part due to the motivation problem), we will still need humans to help students learn, grow, and develop.

t: 6 Leadership Problems That Aren’t What They Look Like
q: At that point, I realized that I had mistaken a dependency problem for a discipline problem, two very different problems with very different solutions.
I find that leadership works the same way, except that most of us like to skip the questions.
Here’s what I’ve noticed and experienced after 20+ years of leading teams: the symptom is what you see or observe around you, but the root cause is what you need to fix.
Just because you didn’t hear any disagreement in a meeting, it doesn’t mean that everyone is committed to the plan.
Silence doesn’t always mean that people feel fearful of speaking up. Sometimes the problem is the room, not the people.
You can’t force empowerment. Your team learns it from what happens after they decide.
If you change the people and the conflict would still exist, then it’s a system problem, not a people problem.
When I look back at those three missed deadlines that I was talking about at the beginning, the fix wasn’t more check-ins. It was a 30-minute conversation with the other team’s manager.

t: 3-Read Friday #127 Cognitive Hot Dogs, Curious Brains, and Atomising Fractions
q: Ben takes a break from his compelling Alpha School series to write a piece that's uncomfortable for anyone who spends much of their time working with AI (i.e., me). He argues that the brain-as-computer model is a warped mirror.

Our minds are feedback-control systems, shaped by millions of years of biological and cultural evolution. Seen that way, AI looks less like a tutor and more like a cognitive hot dog — tempting in the moment, but quietly undermining what schools exist to protect.
I am obsessed with teacher explanations. We all know that a good explanation needs to be clear and concise, but Vicky argues that clarity is the second step, not the first.
Students arrive with mental models that already feel complete. Unless they’re wondering, predicting or wrestling with something before we explain, even our best explanations can land flat.
This week, there have been some cracking posts on practical examples of atomisation. I chose Dylan’s because it got me thinking about a different way to teach adding fractions

t: (Co)video killed the radio star
q: However, explaining all student outcomes away using the pandemic effectively lowers the bar for students

Rather than put in interventions or strengthen our planning to fill the potholes which were created by the pandemic, we instead drive over them and hope for the first it doesn’t hurt our wheel alignment.

t: Writing Has a Framework Problem
q: Effective teaching is not simply the delivery of strategies or programs. It involves making hundreds of instructional decisions, often with incomplete information and in highly complex classroom contexts.
One of the major achievements of these reforms has been their attempt to specify knowledge rather than simply prescribe practice.
A framework can tell us that modelling is important. It cannot tell us what to model for a particular student, at a particular point in time, in response to a particular learning need.
A framework can tell us that feedback matters. It cannot determine whether a student needs feedback on ideas, sentence construction, text structure, spelling, or self-regulation.
Kim’s work is particularly useful because it encourages us to move beyond questions of strategy and towards questions of understanding.
These are not simply pedagogical questions. They are questions about professional reasoning. And professional reasoning depends upon professional knowledge.
Yet these developments sit alongside a striking omission: no widely accepted account of the professional knowledge that underpins teachers’ decisions about writing.

q: There are two ways this happens. The obvious failure is neglect: People skip the process or adopt the tool halfway. But the more dangerous failure is full reversal: People use the practice in a way that undermines the purpose it was designed to serve.
Reversal is more pernicious and harder to notice. Leaders can point to a score or process they believe they are implementing correctly while unknowingly using it backward.
But a stretch goal should create permission to attempt something whose outcome is uncertain. Making a bonus mechanically depend on achieving it converts an experiment into a promise.

Automation makes it easy to turn a score into a cutoff and reject applicants before anyone weighs their experience, work samples, or circumstances. But faster rejection is not necessarily better selection.
Leaders should ask a simple question before adopting the next practice: Does the way we are using this tool still produce the outcome it was meant to create?

t: The corrupting power of workplace ‘power’
q: Power doesn’t change people into someone they weren’t. It amplifies the pre-existing tendencies that were already there, while dismantling the social brakes that kept them in check.

The people at the top of organisations, Obhi’s research suggested, are literally less able (at a neurological level)to take the perspective of the people they lead. They become less accurate at reading emotions from faces.
When we feel powerful, the empathy regions of the brain disengage. We suddenly become more impulsive, more likely to behave inappropriately, and we generally lose touch with other people.

When leaders are not routinely exposed to honest challenge (when the boardroom dynamics have been arranged, consciously or not, to produce deference rather than debate) the empathy deficit goes unnoticed and uncorrected.

By the time a difficult truth reaches the CEO’s desk, it has often been softened, contextualised, or quietly omitted. The leader’s picture of reality becomes progressively more flattering and progressively less accurate.
But they address the symptoms at the individual level while leaving the structural accelerants entirely intact.

The organisations that manage power most effectively are not the ones that trust their leaders’ character. They are the ones that build systems that make good behaviour the path of least resistance, and accountability the default rather than the exception.

t: What If We Started by Naming the Gap?
q: Before we rush to fix a system, perhaps we need to become better at clearly naming the gap between what it says it exists to do and what it is actually producing.
An organization may proudly declare that “people are our greatest asset” while creating conditions that leave its best people chronically depleted.

None of these examples requires us to believe that the people involved are bad or that the institutions themselves are intentionally failing. Often, everyone inside them is doing the best they can within structures that evolved over time.

Clarity is different from outrage. It does not require us to embarrass anyone, demonize people whose views differ from ours, or arrive with the perfect solution already in hand. It asks us to be willing to look at reality and describe it accurately.

Too often, we jump immediately from frustration into competing solutions. Everyone begins arguing over what should happen before we have even developed enough shared understanding about what is happening.
Not because one person can repair an entire system, but because systems are made of patterns, and patterns change when enough people begin participating differently.

t: The Blessing of Living Under Authority

t: My Parents Raised Seven Children, Not Seven Copies
q: My parents, pretty early on, seem to have made the earth-shattering discovery that each of their children were completely different.
Thus, they chose the second option, homeschooling, so that they could nurture each of us in the ways they felt best suited to us and our unique personalities.
While my parents never made us do things we hated, they never let us settle for mediocrity. I liked basketball. My parents pushed me to get as good as I possibly could.
Again, if this seems like a lot of work for my parents, remember they have done this for ALL SEVEN CHILDREN. Each one is different.

We still tease my dad about how often he asked us as kids, “what do you want to do with your life?” It’s funny to picture that serious conversation between a father and his ten-year-old, but it really was such a helpful thing to ask.
I didn’t always know exactly what I wanted to do, but by exploring many things, I for sure knew what I DID NOT want to do. That knowledge was invaluable.
For example, if I was ever a moody teen, my mom would immediately tell me to go outside and practice basketball, because she knew that exercise made me feel better.
My parent’s attention and support made me feel like I had something valuable to contribute to the world and they were going to help me find it.

t: I Spent Thirty Years Believing My Worth Was a Number
q: The two emptiest moments of my life were the two times I got everything I wanted.
I was not building a career. I was building a case for my own existence, and I thought if I made it airtight enough, the fear would finally rest.
I had chosen safe over alive and then gone quiet inside the choice, the way you do when a life looks correct on paper.
It was not my life that was hollow anymore. It was the summit itself.
Everything I was supposed to want equated to nothing I actually needed.
The emptiness was never a defect. It was self-recognition, showing up behind schedule, telling me what I didn’t want to hear.

What finally replaced the number was this: my worth lives in agency, the power to choose what I spend my time on, and in doing work so deeply a part of me that it is what I would be proud to leave as my legacy.

She argues that the emptiness is self-recognition arriving behind schedule, telling you that your worth was never a number or a title.
Her replacement measure is agency, meaning the ability to choose how to spend your time on work that matters to you and that you would be proud to leave behind.

t: Do Analogies Work? How Do We Know?
q: A well-placed analogy can feel like a shortcut. Once we understand one phenomenon, we can start to see connections to others.
Mary Gick and Keith Holyoak conducted fascinating experiments to help answer this question.
The takeaway: Not everyone sees the same kinds of connections. Some people see patterns; others just see teamwork or military exercises.
The results were stark. People who saw the convergence pattern were much more likely to use it in a different situation.
Of the participants in the “good” category, 91% solved the radiation problem (10 of 11 people)
First, when we see a connection, it’s easy to assume that everyone else sees it too. They don’t. Instead of assuming, make the important connections clear.
Second, this kind of knowledge is transferable. Once the audience sees and can describe the pattern, they are more likely to apply it later.

t: Child Poverty Is Down. And Yet So Are Reading Scores.
q: There’s no question that poverty matters for reading outcomes. Children growing up in poverty may face housing instability or food insecurity, and they have less access to books or other educational resources.
But here’s an uncomfortable fact: Child poverty has fallen significantly over time, and yet reading scores have declined anyway.
By that measure, child poverty fell from 20.7% in 2009 to 13.4% in 2025.
But like the national numbers, Michigan has experienced a decline in child poverty. Between 2014 and 2024, the state's child poverty rate fell from 22.6% to 18%, according to Census Bureau data.
In Michigan, average scores fell 8.3 points from 2013 (in blue) to 2024 (in red).
Whatever is driving America's literacy problems, child poverty cannot be the primary explanation.
The gains were modest, but they provide evidence that better reading policies can make a difference.
But children who are struggling to read today can’t afford to wait for policymakers to fully eradicate poverty before tackling reading.

t: Can AI Finally Create Intelligently Varied Practice?
q: However, the results were underwhelming, to say the least. Sure, the LLMs could change one thing, but they did so arbitrarily. I first shared examples and non-examples of what I wanted to create. t: Bring Back Bildung
q: The same people who speak for a 400 billion dollar industry seem to dislike the so-called industrial model of education.
In other words, the Prussian critique is often the sales pitch for what I’ve called the Marketplace Mirror.
Importantly, the whole of this system was designed to support the formation of the individual, free from extrinsic influence, free from politics, war, and industry.
He rejected the necessity for an “intellectual aristocracy” and believed that the most ordinary labourer and the most privileged socialite must begin from the same foundation.

He argued that mixing them produced neither complete human beings nor complete citizens. His example was in teaching arithmetic: if you teach a child to count and compute using coins, mathematics becomes tied to commerce, shopping, and transactional value from the outset.
He believed that education should aim at the student as a whole person, not at the role they might fill in society.
Bildung shifted from a universal ideal to the marker of a credentialed and educated middle class. It became an instrument of selection, rather than one of freedom.
Industry looks different today, but it’s still industry. Humboldt was concerned by the state, but his logic holds for any power that wants a predetermined product from its schools.

t: Brain Training Works. Just Not the Way You Hoped.
q: Here is the part the advert leaves out. The games work. That was never the problem. The problem is what they work on.
By the end, people had gotten better at every task they practised. On the tasks they had not practised, even ones that looked like close cousins of the trained games, nothing had moved at all.

When you drill a task, the brain genuinely changes, but it changes in a stubbornly specific place. The networks that particular task leans on get more efficient, and the gain stays bolted to them, doing that one job.

Show a chess master a real game position for a few seconds, and they will rebuild it from memory almost perfectly. Scatter the same pieces at random, and they are barely better than someone who learned the moves last week.

Gather up nearly ninety of those studies and the picture holds still. Train, and your scores on the working-memory tasks go up, at least for a while. But the jump everyone is actually paying for, into sharper reasoning and better schoolwork, never arrives.
Getting fast and accurate at chopping an onion makes you good at chopping onions. It does not travel across to your handwriting, even though both are just your hand.
Year after year of broad, effortful learning that is always a little too hard, the kind that makes a child think in ways they would never have picked for themselves. No game has come close.

t: Atomising Fraction Addition
q: Take a concept, break it into small pieces, teach one piece at a time, and build up to the larger concept. I find the idea helpful, but I have also found it to be much harder in practice than it sounds.
The core of atomisation, to me, is managing cognitive load. Students have finite working memory capacity: we can only hold a few things in our mind at once.
Students are thinking hard about multiplication, not about the meaning of fractions and why we add them the way we do, which means they’re less likely to retain that learning.
It relies on skip-counting, which my students are pretty confident with, rather than jumping straight to multiplication.
Instead I have them do a few, then the next day check for understanding and do a few more, and continue that until students can reliably remember how to do this the next day.
The second benefit is that, with less cognitive demand, it’s much easier to step back and make connections.
When I don’t break math down into small steps, some students are so overwhelmed that they lose both the details and the big picture.
If I’m managing cognitive load effectively, that frees up mental energy that we can spend making connections and thinking about big ideas.

Both standard fraction addition methods depend on multiplication, so students with weak facts spend their working memory on arithmetic rather than on what fractions mean.

t: Aristotle's Poetics: Final Project
q: Plot is properly of first importance in regard to the components of a story for the obvious reason that Plot is to Character as Water is to Fish. The Plot forms the world wherein the characters of the story can live and move and have their being.
A story with no structure, no intentional arrangement of the incidents meant to bring about a certain conclusion, is aimless and conveys little meaning.
Functionally he suggests cutting anything extraneous, that which does not support or advance the plot toward the end or which really properly belongs to another story other than the one being told.

Thought is the manifestation of a character’s reasoning which undergirds their actions in the story.

Ideally, however, Spectacle is meant to support, not supplant, the story the writer has made. A good play or movie does not subvert the role of story-telling for the sake of mere spectacular effects.

t: Always Prioritise Your Health, Then Your Team’s

t: Adam Grant on How to Vibe
q: I’ve found that we need three kinds of people: allies, pals, and companions. Allies are people who share our goals: we’re on a mission together.

You’re more likely to get a job through distant friends than close friends. It’s not just due to numbers; the people you don’t know well are more likely to know about new opportunities and open new doors.

Different situations bring out different sides of us. My favorite example is Dwight Schrute on The Office: if he’s with a subordinate, then he’s domineering, but if he’s with a superior, he’s deferential.
Strong bonds can survive months or even years of distance. It’s common, though, for people to mistake a lapse in communication for a lack of care.
Respectful disagreement can bring us closer together—it signals that we care enough about one another’s opinions to put energy into trying to change them.
To paraphrase Bob Burg, people who take pride in being brutally honest are mostly interested in being brutal. Be direct in what you say but kind in how you say it.

t: AI's Real Value Is Upstream
q: But the much bigger opportunity is upstream, in the CEO’s strategic work: setting direction, allocating resources, making decisions, and keeping the organization focused on its goals.

But if you point it at a company where priorities live in the CEO’s head, accountability is fuzzy, and decisions get remade every week, it will produce more disorder at greater speed and with more confidence.
I call this leadership by ESP. The CEO communicates something broad, people try to infer the intended meaning, and the organization moves forward based on a collection of educated guesses.
The better your people are, the less you need to dictate their methods. But you still need to give them clear objectives, appropriate authority, and enough context to make good decisions.

t: A Conversation with James V. Shuls: Restoring the Purpose of American Education
q: Education is the formation of a person. We want students formed with character, rooted in our traditions and our history, and with a right-ordered faith in the principles that our nation was built upon.
Today, we seem to have lost this understanding. Education is seen as the activities that take place in school—reading, writing, and arithmetic—or as a means of preparing students for the workforce.
The fact that we even question the role of truth, goodness, and character formation in public schools is an indictment of our modern concept of public education.
When my son entered first grade, I asked his teachers a simple question: “What’s the best book my child will read this year?” The response was appalling: “Whatever he likes.
Rather than demanding submission, the state should help parents exercise their responsibility to educate their children.
School leaders and board members, whether in public or private institutions, can set the direction of a school.

t: What I learned listening to a principal coach
q: Most of us have sat through a coaching conversation with an administrator. Some leave you energized; others leave you feeling processed.

In the one-on-one sessions, up to 75 percent of her questions were open-ended, and she sat beside teachers rather than across a desk. In one committee meeting, 91 percent of her questions were closed, and directive language outnumbered collaborative language 12 to 1.

The structure didn’t decide the conversation; the moment did. And under time pressure, reflection didn’t just shrink. It disappeared, which means the parts of coaching most tied to teacher growth were the first to go.

t: What Aristotle Can Teach America
q: What if the problem with America is not “out there” manifested in our political opponents or a rigged system, but internally, with us?

We moderns tend to think of it exclusively in reference to satisfying our desires, but the Greeks’ conception of the term focused on ethical virtue and contemplating the good; in other words, aligning our thoughts and actions with what is objectively good
Thus, virtue is not only some sort of stoic program of self-improvement but is foundational to the political life.
As many scholars of the American founding have argued, liberty was never intended by the founders as “license,” meaning the freedom to do anything. Instead, it gave the opportunity to achieve virtue.
As Blitz perceptively observes, for all of the talk of American government and law being dispassionate and neutral, it is impossible for both not to form a certain character.
It is for this reason that “legislating morality” is impossible to avoid, because all law is based in morality.

Many of us are too proud (or self-righteous) to acknowledge that it is we who need to repent and improve as much as it is those who lead us.

t: There’s No Excuse For a Dirty, Disorganized Home
q: No amount of organization or help can root out bitterness. Even if you hired a maid, that person would not be able to clean the inside of a soul. It evinces a deeper spiritual problem.
First, some basic expectations. Spotlessness is not necessarily the goal. A perfect house, ready for a photoshoot, is not the goal. Joyful, righteous living is the goal.
Rather, the home should be well-enough kept that the family, at the drop of a hat, can spend about 30 minutes and be prepared to invite guests inside the door without being embarrassed.
Children are an asset. As such, they require some up-front investment. If you invest properly, they can be more valuable than you can possibly imagine.
The conversation is the point, and the husband needs to lead it, with input from his wife. Usually this doesn’t need to take longer than 15 minutes. Then put the list on the refrigerator.

Your household needs a mission beyond rest and entertainment. Something bigger than yourself, something you would not be able to accomplish alone. It can be as simple as radical hospitality, where you commit to having people over at least once per week or more.
Now, chores become part of something larger. Every sweep of the broom is in service to loving your neighbor. Every scrub of the toilet means something beyond the smell of bleach.
x: Franklin of Foundation Father argues that a messy home is a spiritual and leadership problem before it is an organizational one, and he addresses both husband and wife.

Children can be taught and supervised to do real household work, and the up-front investment pays off because they are an asset to the family.

t: The Convenient Argument
q: Dear reader, if you’ve found yourself defending your commitment to a value when all you did was question a practice, I’m afraid someone has rather quietly changed the subject.
Incorrect. Direct Instruction (capital D; capital I) involves using a script. “Explicit and direct instruction” does not have to.

Of course, these caricatures aren’t real. Sure, it’s quite likely desks are in rows for most learning, and there’s a good chance there’s some rote memorisation included, but would you believe you can do all of those things and still run a lesson that’s responsive to students in the room and even fun?
But there’s a rather important difference between using provocative language to draw attention to an argument and using it to do the arguing for you.
Believe it or not, you can care about academics and still prioritise wellbeing. In fact, I’d go as far as to say I focus on teaching academics well as part of my prioritisation of student wellbeing.

This shifts the debate. It’s not about the relative merits of different instructional approaches anymore. Now the conversation is about whether you care about students, value their individuality, respect their autonomy or believe they deserve exposure to “real world” problems.

Rather than defending the evidence for a practice, the writer gets to defend a value nobody was disputing in the first place. And the person asking perfectly reasonable questions about effectiveness is left explaining that they do, in fact, care about children.

However, to actually have those discussions, they require us to represent opposing positions accurately, distinguish practices from values, and engage with what people actually believe, rather than what we would prefer them to believe.
x: Semantic substitution turns a question about a practice, such as restorative conversations versus consequences, into an accusation that the questioner opposes the value itself.

The caricature turns an advocate of explicit instruction into a rigid, scripted, joyless figure, and she distinguishes capital-D Direct Instruction, which uses scripts, from explicit teaching, which need not.
Caiti Wade of The Disruptive Educator uses a rereading of Jane Austen as a frame for showing how critics of explicit instruction win arguments nobody was making.
Loaded language and provocative headlines can do the arguing for a writer, so readers should check the underlying report before reacting to the framing.
False dichotomies such as academics versus wellbeing recast a debate about instructional effectiveness as a debate about whether you care about children.

t: The Confidence Trap
q: Being extraordinary at a job and being effective at managing people who do that job are related but distinct skill sets, and conflating them is one of the most reliable ways to simultaneously lose a great individual contributor and gain a mediocre leader.
We are, as a species, extraordinarily bad at distinguishing between confidence and competence and our selection processes make the problem significantly worse.
The same cognitive skills needed to perform a task well are the ones needed to recognise when you’re performing it badly.
Traditional job interviews are, the evidence suggests, remarkably good at doing one thing: identifying people who are good at interviews.
Decisiveness looks like leadership. Certainty reads as authority.
Over time, that calcifies into a culture where admitting uncertainty is career-limiting, which is precisely the culture in which the worst decisions get made.

360-degree assessment, where candidates are evaluated by peers, direct reports, and those they report to, reduces the overconfidence premium significantly. It is harder to project false certainty to people who work alongside you every day.
The most dangerous leader in any organisation is not the one who doesn’t know the answers.
x: Organisations select managers mostly on past performance in an unrelated role, which is why excellent engineers or salespeople so often struggle as leaders.
Rewarding confidence over competence teaches employees that certainty beats curiosity and makes admitting uncertainty career-limiting.
Ghassan Karian argues that organisations routinely promote the wrong people into leadership because they mistake confidence for competence.
Traditional interviews, he says, mainly identify people who are good at interviews, and most firms also promote on past functional performance rather than leadership potential.

Rewarding confidence over competence teaches employees that certainty beats curiosity and makes admitting uncertainty career-limiting.
Structured competency-based assessment, 360-degree input and blind shortlisting reduce the charisma premium and are far more predictive than gut-feel interviews.

t: Teacher Workflow No. 04: the book half your students never bought
q: The bookstore wants your spring adoptions, and on most campuses the easiest thing to do is click “same as last term.
This workflow finds that third and swaps the rest for free material you’ve checked yourself. Students get a course reader that answers their questions with citations.
Any chapter where you cannot write that line is the first one to replace.
Chat tools can invent sources with total confidence, including real-looking links to books that don’t exist.
Anything that fails one check comes off the list. A candidate you have not opened does not exist.
Replacing half the book with material you trust beats replacing all of it with material you guessed at.
Don’t replace the whole book. Run steps 1 through 3 on the one chapter you already skip half of, and swap that chapter alone.
x: The premise is that many students go weeks without the book and instructors rarely use more than a third of it, yet the easy path at adoption time is to click same as last term.
Doan Winkel's How to Teach With AI series offers a five-step workflow for replacing most of an expensive assigned textbook with free, verified material and a course reader.
The workflow starts by naming the job each chapter does in the course, so that chapters with no clear job are the first to be replaced.

In steps one to three the instructor uses a chat tool to map what job each chapter does, to find open-licensed candidates for each job, and then opens every link personally because chat tools invent sources with total confidence.
Every AI-suggested source must be opened and checked for existence, open license and fit, because a candidate the instructor has not opened should be treated as nonexistent.

t: Research Bite #80: Understanding Verbal Probability Expressions
q: Uncertain scientific information is often communicated with words such as “likely” or “rarely” in place of numbers. This study asked how secondary school students in England turn those words into numbers.
Students disagreed most on words at the extremes (”certain”, “impossible”) and on words for events that are more likely than not (”very likely”, “usually”).
Students in this study read probability words less strongly than adults do, and they disagreed with each other a lot. “Certain” averaged 83% and “impossible” averaged 13%.
If you tell a class that an outcome is “very likely”, add a percentage or a fraction so they know how strong a claim you are making.
Spend lesson time agreeing what probability words mean. The authors point out that teachers rarely teach these words because they presume students already know them.

Students placed it at about 53%, close to “maybe”, while “impossible” sat near the bottom of the scale. So a student who hears “it’s possible the experiment will fail” may take that as roughly an even chance.
Choosing one or two words per group and using them consistently across maths and science gives students fewer meanings to guess at.
This was a one-off questionnaire in five schools in the South of England, and the authors had limited means of checking students engaged.
x: The study asked 184 students in five English schools to place 29 probability words on a slider from 0 to 100 percent.
Students interpret probability words less strongly than adults and disagree widely, so a teacher's very likely may land well below what was meant.

Pairing a word with a percentage or fraction removes ambiguity when the exact chance matters.

The word possible was read as roughly an even chance, so teachers should say plainly when they mean it could happen but probably will not.

t: Remaining Human-Centered in the Age of AI
a: Teaching in the Age of AI
q: AI is already an environment in which we are immersed, as well as a force with which we must engage.
Smart technology is now ambient. At this point, if you don’t want to use or be exposed to AI, you have to actively avoid many of the ways it’s already seeped into our lives.
The problem is that the gulf between what’s possible with AI in schools and the national conversation around it makes it likely that we will overcorrect toward bans.

The actual task in front of schools is harder and less satisfying than a black-and-white policy. It’s this: Figuring out what to protect and how to prepare, and doing both in a way parents can see and believe in.

Producing an essay is not the main purpose of writing one. Sitting with a thought, spinning it out in different directions, and reworking it until it’s clear enough to be understood by someone else is a lifelong practice.
Restrictions can protect learning, but Anderson is right that they cannot substitute for teaching students to understand AI.
Educating people about the use of AI, then, involves teaching them to decide when and for what purpose it ought not to be used.
Most of the schools I know have rules about AI by now. Very few have a curriculum.
x: He worries that the recent turn against screens and AI in schools, including New York City's one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI through eighth grade, will overcorrect toward bans.
Smart technology has become ambient, so avoiding AI now takes active effort and a technology-free school bubble is not realistic.
