t: Progressive Hangovers
q: Without the anchor of the past, progressive education became a shapeshifting organism whose goals, methods, and metrics exist in a constant state of flux. And for a while, this organism had a monopoly on education in America.
With a limited number of guiding texts, classical ed meant things like socratic discussion, grammar-stage-logic-stage-rhetoric-stage, and teaching how to think instead of what to think.
However, these implementations were added as modifications to the existing school model… a largely progressive model.
At the risk of generalization, progressive education assumes that the same education is fit for all. It is a leveler which, unfortunately, tends toward the lowest common denominator.
The top third are frequently bored, the bottom third are overwhelmed, and the middle third are somewhere in between, depending on the day.

Classical educators are already experimenting with new structures for the school day: there exist already classical co-ops, in person or online, university-model schools, Charlotte Mason schools, single-sex schools or classrooms, forest schools, and go-live-on-a-farm schools.

In one sense, tailoring education to individual needs is a very progressive idea. However, what the classical tradition knows, which progressives lost, is that many of the individual’s needs are met by tradition and the liberal arts.
x: The first generation of classical educators came from progressive schools and bolted Socratic discussion and the trivium stages onto an existing progressive model, which he honors but says must be moved past.

He argues that progressive education treats all students alike and tends toward the lowest common denominator, while the Western Christian paideia accepts unequal strengths and diverse formation.
Samuel Sadler argues that the classical Christian school movement, for all its progress, is still carrying inherited progressive assumptions that it should deliberately shed.

t: Of Course, Kids Are Distracted in Class. But It’s an Easier Fix Than We Think.
q: There is an attention crisis in Canada’s public schools. Thanks to overly lenient and inconsistent phone policies, along with an enthusiastic embrace of educational technology, we have created conditions that make it more difficult than ever for students to focus on learning, which happens to be the point of going to school.

The obvious solution is for all provincial education departments to mandate a strict bell-to-bell phone ban that physically separates students from their devices for the duration of the school day, including lunch and recess.
It may feel convenient for the teacher who saves time and paper, but it’s inconvenient for the student who must fend off (or succumb to) distraction while reading the assignment on their phone.
Instead, teams can use an e-mail newsletter, a Google document, a regularly updated website, a group messaging app that is accessible from a computer or even an old-fashioned bulletin board.
Furthermore, offering screen-based play as a reward can motivate a child to rush through their work in order to get to the device.
These few simple changes won’t solve the broader problem of superfluous EdTech and phones in schools, but they can help reinforce teachers in the continuing battle for students’ attention.
x: A provincial bell-to-bell phone ban, including lunch and recess, is her preferred fix, and she says U.S. schools that adopted one report strong results.
A provincial bell-to-bell phone ban, including lunch and recess, is her preferred fix, and she says U.S. schools that adopted one report strong results.
Martinko frames classroom distraction as the predictable result of loose phone rules combined with heavy ed-tech use, backed by data on off-task laptop time.
Keeping teams and clubs off Instagram and Snapchat protects families who are trying to delay social media, and plain email or a website serves the same purpose.
Screen-based games and device time as a reward undercut focus, and she cites Prodigy's own figure of 888 questions to raise a test score by one point.
She admits these will not solve the broader problem of superfluous ed-tech and phones, yet argues they send a clear signal that learning outranks administrative convenience.

t: Observations on the Reform of Catholic High School Education https://primematters.com/index.php/perspectives/observations-reform-catholic-high-school-education
q: At its core, the standard Great Books approach has an Enlightenment anthropology. We expose students to “the great conversation” with all its pitfalls, and leave the student to make what sense he can of it in a community of other readers.

Rather than a Great Books approach, I propose that a Catholic school’s main task is to form students in a vision of reality permeated by the Incarnation. It is a sacramental vision that recognizes that “the world is charged with the grandeur of God
There is a danger in collapsing the Church’s educational apostolate into “making saints.

For Newman, the end of liberal education is seeing the whole of reality. Philosophical knowledge (not the academic discipline of philosophy) is a form of knowledge that synthesizes the views of particular disciplines into a coherent vision of all of reality.

Indeed, I would go so far as to say that most of the time given to traditional philosophy in a Catholic classical school ought to be given to literature and history, and that courses in Catholic doctrine should be less abstract and more literary and historical.

We learn to live a good life by imitation. A central intellectual task for a student to develop in high school is how doctrines, which, again, are true abstractions from scripture, can be seen embodied, incarnated, in particular lives.

It is not that we bring the students into a “great conversation” but rather that we judiciously use “the best that has been thought and said in the world” (including pagan and “heretical” texts but with a preponderance of Catholic texts) to both form and bring students to a Catholic vision of reality.
x: But he argues the standard Great Books approach carries an Enlightenment anthropology that treats students as unfallen, neutral individuals sampling a great conversation, which breeds cynicism.
A Catholic school's main task is to form students in a sacramental vision of reality permeated by the Incarnation, not to induct them into a great conversation.

He distinguishes the immediate end of Catholic liberal education, in Newman's sense of seeing the whole of reality, from its ultimate end of salvation, warning against collapsing the school's task into making saints.
He separates the immediate end of liberal education, knowledge and seeing reality whole, from the ultimate end of salvation, and warns against collapsing a school into a saint-making institution.
He concludes that more school time should go to literature and history than to abstract philosophy, preparing the way for God to make saints.
Drawing on Lewis, Tolkien, Aristotle and Aquinas, he says the imagination presents the good through particulars, so doctrine should be seen incarnated in lives.
A Catholic school's main task is to form students in a sacramental vision of reality permeated by the Incarnation, not to induct them into a great conversation.

t: Is Teaching a Science or a Craft?
q: It’s one of those arguments that sounds important until you realise it’s actually a false dichotomy. Teaching isn’t one or the other; it’s both.

Also, calling teaching a knack trivialises it while at the same time conveniently excusing schools of education, school districts, and governments from the hard work of systematically developing and supporting it.
Cognitive psychology matters because teaching that ignores how people learn is always going to be weaker than teaching that works with human cognition rather than against it.
This is where things get interesting, because craft is not the opposite of science. It’s what happens when scientific knowledge is enacted, adapted, and refined in real classrooms.
Craft is not vague intuition. It’s knowledge (the scientific knowledge) in action; wisdom.
Put simply, the science can be (and should be) taught quite explicitly at the outset; the craft has to be cultivated and developed through guided experience.
If we assume teaching is mainly craft, we risk underpreparing teachers scientifically and leaving them to pick things up by trial and error or use their gut feelings/common (non)sense.
Without craft, teaching can become rigid, mechanical, and oddly inhuman, as though knowing the research were enough to tell us what to do in the classroom.
x: Paul Kirschner and Nidhi Sachdeva take on the long-running debate over whether teaching is a science or a craft and call it a false dichotomy.
Treating teaching as a natural knack excuses institutions from the systematic work of preparing and supporting teachers.
Treating teaching as a natural knack excuses institutions from the systematic work of preparing and supporting teachers.
Craft is the practical wisdom that emerges when that knowledge is enacted, adapted and refined in real classrooms.
Craft is the practical wisdom that emerges when that knowledge is enacted, adapted and refined in real classrooms.
The authors argue that initial teacher education should teach the science explicitly, while craft is cultivated over time through induction, mentoring, reflection and guided experience.
The science of teaching rests on five building blocks: subject knowledge, how we learn, how we teach, what we use and how we relate.
They warn that without science teaching drifts toward myths and eminence-based fads, and without craft it becomes rigid and mechanical.

t: How to Grow Comprehension
q: Our continued desire for measurement precision, predictive ability, and guarantees with reading comprehension is so off, it’s not even wrong. While we can identify and measure some of the elements that contribute to comprehension, we cannot precisely predict or guarantee the understanding that results from their interaction.

Like with grass growing, there is science to back up these elements. The question, then, is: How do we translate what we know about the science of reading comprehension into instructional and assessment practices that actually support its growth?

But instead of recognizing that comprehension depends on the interaction of multiple elements, features, and conditions, we've designed our instruction and assessment around mastering individual standards.
That’s like trying to grow grass by only focusing on your watering schedule and ignoring everything else. The result for reading is superficial comprehension. That’s our weedy lawn.
This means that designing units and lessons must start with studying the texts, not identifying the standards students need to master.

Rather than committing to a particular instructional approach like direct instruction or discovery-based learning, we focused on which approach or combination of approaches would best equip students with the knowledge and habits of thinking to comprehend each text.
Their scores represented how each student handled that specific text for that specific purpose at that specific moment.

Our systems have slowly led us away from the learning we care about toward what we can most easily measure. Since comprehension is complex and hard to measure, we’ve substituted mastery of discrete skills as evidence of understanding, even as students still struggle to read and understand complex, grade-level texts.
x: Because the reader, the text and the purpose change each time, comprehension cannot be precisely measured, predicted or guaranteed, just as no gauge guarantees that grass will grow.
Whitney Whealdon continues her lawn metaphor for reading instruction by asking how the science of reading comprehension can be turned into classroom practice that actually grows understanding.
Rather than committing to direct instruction or discovery, designers should choose the approach, such as read aloud, paired reading or think aloud, that fits the conditions of each text.
Teaching standards as a checklist of separable skills is like fixing only the watering schedule of a lawn, and it yields superficial comprehension.
Lesson design should begin with the text, asking what makes it challenging, what knowledge it requires and which relationships among ideas are hard to spot.
Rather than committing to direct instruction or discovery, designers should choose the approach, such as read aloud, paired reading or think aloud, that fits the conditions of each text.
A single assessment score reflects one reader, one text and one purpose, so teachers should read results as one piece of a longer comprehension profile.
Comprehension is an active process of connecting a text to existing knowledge, so the understanding a reader stores is unique and cannot be guaranteed by any single lesson or test.

t: How Leaders Can Build Judgment, Not Just Expertise
q: Expertise tells you how something works. Judgment tells you what matters most when the facts are incomplete, the goals are mixed, and no rule quite fits the situation.
Leaders who confuse expertise and judgment end up with teams full of capable specialists who flounder the moment a situation falls outside the conventional playbook.

The contract is one input to the credit decision, not the decision itself. Judgment requires holding several considerations all at once and choosing a response that the organization can stand behind later.
Leaders build judgment by exposing team members to how decisions get made, not just to how tasks get done.
They ask team members, “What would you do and why?” and then talk through their own reasoning, including what they gave weight to and what they chose to give up.
The best test of a leader’s influence is not what the team knows. It is how the team decides when the answer is not in the field manual.
Expertise makes people useful. Judgment makes them trustworthy. Good leaders build both.
x: Expertise answers known questions, whereas judgment weighs mixed goals and incomplete facts, and treating them as the same leaves teams of specialists who flounder off the playbook.
Expertise answers known questions, whereas judgment weighs mixed goals and incomplete facts, and treating them as the same leaves teams of specialists who flounder off the playbook.
The credit-dispute example shows that a contract is one input to a decision, not the decision itself.
Asking team members what they would do and why, then debriefing, builds a way of thinking one conversation at a time.
Leaders can grow judgment by explaining the trade-offs behind their decisions, including what they gave weight to and what they gave up.
The measure of a leader's influence is how the team decides when the leader is not in the room.
This Admired Leadership Field Note argues that organizations are very good at building expertise but far less deliberate about building judgment.

t: Forming the Affections of Our Children
q: Informed by our faith, we believe that beauty, truth, and goodness exist for their own sake, and the pursuit of these transcendentals is a gift.
Poetry had become part of his lived experience, and he reached for it when no other form of communication could do justice to what he was seeing.
Yet once in a while, children reveal the work that years of formation have been quietly striving to accomplish.
Children are capable of encountering beauty before they understand the concepts behind beauty. My son did not understand the Dickinson poem, but he did not need to understand it.

Perhaps the point of memorizing poetry for young children is not so that they can recite it on command and impress their friends and relatives. Perhaps it is for poetry to arise unbidden when reality calls for it.

Their taste is something that can be formed deliberately, and if we simply leave their taste up to the vagaries of life, plenty of clamoring voices will chime in to grab their attention and form their souls.
Parents of young children, and especially of young men, have a duty to show them what is truly worth having in their repertoire of knowledge and experience.
x: Paul Kearney, a former classical-school elementary teacher and now a father, tells how his three-year-old son responded to a mountain view by asking for the Emily Dickinson poem about statures touching the sky.
A three-year-old reaching for a Dickinson poem at a mountain overlook illustrates how early poetry becomes part of a child's lived experience of reality.
Children can delight in beauty before they understand the concepts behind it, so delight comes before meaning in formation.
Children can delight in beauty before they understand the concepts behind it, so delight comes before meaning in formation.
In his view the purpose of memorizing poems with small children is not performance but to have poetry arise unbidden when reality calls for it.
Because young children are malleable, their tastes can be deliberately formed, and if parents leave it to chance, competing voices will form their souls.
Parents have a duty to introduce children, and especially boys, to the simple beauties that enrich the soul, even amid the survival mode of ordinary family life.

t: Community Incarnates Classical Education
q: Skills must be acquired, and diplomas are practical, but “to know self” and see God requires stronger stuff. A school is not a fundamental social category. We need families and the church.

Without a strong community grounded in the past and serving the area, consistent with the values of family, church, we can get lost. We come unmoored. Canonical education naturally helps with this problem.
Sometimes we even boast of the separation of “town and gown”. Townies are stereotyped as servants at best and barbarians at worst. “Gownies” are sneered at as useless parasites on the community.
A virtuous community is one that enables members to flourish and strengthens virtuous ties to family, church, and the broader community.
A community exists to help humans flourish, not books in libraries, buildings, or any other stuff.
The school that laughs at itself will not easily fall for “consultants” or other flimflam men who so infect education.

Celebrate the alma mater, and the graduates will be celebrated as members of that community. Make sure that, from the very start of a college or school, there is a book they can sign or a wall where names are placed as each generation of teachers and graduates come and go.
x: A classical school needs a living community of customs, place and people, because a canon alone does not keep students from becoming unmoored.
Classical learning can isolate scholars from the surrounding town, so a virtuous school community should deliberately strengthen ties to family, church and neighbors.
Schools should love their place, open their campuses appropriately to the town, and treat members as the reason for the community rather than as means.
Schools should love their place, open their campuses appropriately to the town, and treat members as the reason for the community rather than as means.
John Mark Reynolds argues that classical education needs a living community, not just a canon, to keep students rooted and keep them from coming unmoored.
Whimsy and laughter, along with rituals such as signing a book or marking names on a wall, protect a school from fashionable consultants and root graduates in the alma mater.

t: Christian Education, Character, and Wisdom
q: My working definition of education is “the deliberate formation of a person.

Plato uses the word paideia to describe what we call education. In his Republic, Plato says that paideia refers to the process of a person being turned towards the true, the good, and the beautiful. This means that education is not just downloading information or simply increasing in knowledge.

Education is a training, but it is training for the soul rather than the body. It is the deliberate formation of a person through discipline, training, and instruction, where the person is directed towards the true, the good, and the beautiful.
From this came a tradition of Christian education we now call “classical.” Understood this way, Christian education is classical education.

The aim of education is not knowledge, aesthetic sensitivity, good manners, or good taste. The aim is character. The aim is to form students of good character, to train, disciple, and form good people.
Everyone has a character, but not everyone is virtuous. Your character is whatever you are, and what you are can be made up of virtuous characteristics or vicious ones.

Without wisdom, you cannot have good character, which is the main point of Christian education. It is wisdom that undergirds the desire for, and ability to choose, the true, the good, and the beautiful.
x: Everyone has a character but not everyone is virtuous, so virtues are the parts of character that education must deliberately train.
He defines education as the deliberate formation of a person and roots the idea in the Greek paideia, which Plato describes as turning the soul toward the true, the good and the beautiful.
Education is defined as the deliberate formation of a person toward an aim, which ties it to the Greek idea of paideia and a purpose beyond information transfer.
Christian education descends from the early church's adoption of paideia, which is why the author calls it classical education.
Drawing on Aristotle, Charlotte Mason and James Arthur, he says the aim of education is not knowledge, taste or manners but good character, which is the settled disposition behind virtuous action.
Everyone has a character but not everyone is virtuous, so virtues are the parts of character that education must deliberately train.
Because wise people choose the good, wisdom is the foundation of character, and he supports the point with 2 Peter 1 and Proverbs 1.

t: Billionaires Are Getting Medals. What’s Our Prize?
q: If there’s one thing the executives I talk with agree on about AI, it’s that almost no one has a handle on the bill, let alone the ROI.

If we try to reach “breakeven” on AI through cost-cutting, employment and wages plummet, the economy takes a nose-dive, and the bill never actually gets covered (not to mention the massive unrest). In this Prisoner’s Dilemma, we all go to prison.

Accounting and tax rules are partly to blame. We capitalize and depreciate investments in technology but expense training, so building software doesn’t hit short-term results the way developing people does.
About 75% had made cuts tied to AI, yet “9 in 10 would rethink cuts related to AI if they were given the chance,” and 32% said they’d lost critical skills.
Every round of cuts like this also teaches the people who stay that AI is something done to them rather than for them, and resistance grows.

q: Writers and other intellectuals are people too—they too must eat, do laundry, keep children alive, perhaps even vacuum on occasion. We all are bodies, as well as minds and souls.

I get to tell them that there are seasons, and God wants you to use your gifts, including your academic gets, for the church, but that we don’t have to feel the pressure to lean into all of these gifts at the same time.

t: AI and Spiritual Evolution
q: There is another side to thinking and learning that is harder to capture and measure. This is the experience of insight: the moment when something that was previously obscure suddenly becomes clear.
Because so much of education has been built around print, we have come to mistake the skills of print literacy for intelligence itself.
There is an important distinction here between the living process of understanding and the products it leaves behind.

Much of education focuses on these products: concepts, procedures, explanations and arguments. We turn the living process of discovery into fixed forms of knowledge that can be transmitted and assessed.
Spirit is our lived openness to a larger reality, a relationship with possibilities of meaning that draw us beyond ourselves.

AI is particularly good at handling the products of past understanding: texts, concepts, arguments and explanations. If it can take on more of this, schools could give much more time to the parts of education that bring understanding to life, such as inquiry, discussion, observation, making things and wondering about the world.

t: What even is cognitive activation?
q: Through these questions, the OECD have identified different teaching styles. Three of these are ‘teacher-directed’, ‘student-oriented’ and ‘cognitive activation’. That third category is weird. It sounds more like a prerequisite for learning than a teaching style.

Indeed, in their PISA 2025 report, the OECD authors claim that, ‘In science, [cognitive activation] practices overlap with inquiry-based teaching, where students are encouraged to ask questions, formulate hypotheses, interpret evidence and reflect on conclusions’. That’s quite something given that they previously found a negative association between inquiry learning and PISA science scores.

Buried in an excel sheet in the basement of the latest PISA report is a table showing the different questions the OECD asked to create its index of cognitive activation and the association between each question and performance on the science PISA assessment.
What do you notice? Questions 1, 3 and 4 are exactly what you might expect to see in a class driven by interactive explicit teaching.

Given all the noise about memorisation in previous rounds of PISA—there was a Scientific American article on the woes of memorisation in maths that I criticised many moons ago—I find it surprising both that this sits in a definition of ‘cognitive activation’ and that this finding has passed unremarked by the OECD.

The question that is making up the numbers, with no statistically significant association with achievement, is the one about asking students to explain how they would design an experiment. Oddly enough, this would seem to be the one most relevant to PISA science questions.
Even so, a good foundation of knowledge is probably better preparation than anything else.

t: Three Ironclad Laws of Skill Formation
q: Much of AI and ed tech is about taking shortcuts; ingesting fast food for the body, mind, and soul. They evade what we all know deep down to be true: becoming good at anything requires consistent practice over a period of time; practice should be spaced out; and improvement doesn’t appear overnight.
Skills form through consistent practice over a period of time until it becomes a habit.
As you are developing the habit, low intensity is better than high intensity.
Practice works best when spread out. In other words, spaced practice beats cramming.
Spaced practice is one of the most well-established “known knowns” in learning science.
Progress doesn’t arrive in proportion to effort. This is the hardest lesson to swallow.
Most of what’s being peddled in the marketplace is a waste of time and money unless they support, or at least recognize, the Three Ironclad Laws of Skill Formation.

t: Setting Multiple Priorities Lets Leaders Off the Hook
q: In many organizations, leaders proudly communicate five priorities, 10 strategic imperatives, eight critical success factors, and a host of KPIs and OKRs.
The problem is that naming everything a priority is itself a decision, and usually the wrong one.
When a leader says, “Everything is a priority,” then nothing comes first or is more important than anything else.
But the etymology suggests something else entirely. The real problem is a refusal to choose, and refusing to choose is usually about protection.
The question every leader who creates multiple priorities must ask is, “What am I avoiding and losing by refusing to name one?
Elevating a single priority doesn’t mean nothing else can or should take place. It simply highlights the one thing that must receive the lion’s share of the team’s attention and focus right now.

t: Local by Default, Escalated by Rule
q: A decision that should take a day takes six weeks. Not because it is hard. Because no one can say whose it is, so it travels. Up for comfort, sideways for consensus, into a forum for cover.

t: Formative Writing: Writing to Discover What You Think
q: Instead of asking students to write only when they are ready to prove what they already know, we ask them to write in order to find out what they think.
Formative Writing, by contrast, happens earlier in the cognitive process. It is brief, informal, low-stakes writing used midstream during reading to help students explore and construct meaning.

When we ask students to speak before they have had time to process, we are asking them to perform working-memory acrobatics; recalling text details, structuring an argument, and choosing precise vocabulary all in a fraction of a second.
Because we write at roughly one-tenth the speed of speech, slowing down gives the brain time to access precise academic vocabulary and complex ideas that are still in the process of being mastered.
Frame prompts with words like might or could (“Why might Ralph react so fiercely here?” or “What could the symbol represent?”) to lower the barrier to entry and invite safe intellectual risk-taking.
Hesitant or quiet students have a written safety net to refer to, allowing them to speak with far greater thoroughness and assurance.
By making space for students to “think in writing,” we teach them that writing isn’t just a test of what they already know, it is the ultimate engine for understanding.
x: They distinguish it from summative writing, where students must already know their argument, and cite Joan Didion's remark that she writes to find out what she is thinking.

Writing before talking reduces the working-memory load of speaking on the spot and gives hesitant students a written safety net.

And perhaps more importantly, it reminds us why a phonics screening score is a screening measure rather than a complete judgement about a child’s reading.
It means that roughly one in nine children is still not reaching the phonics standard by the end of Year 2.

t: 17 Maxims for a Good Life
q: Learning asks you to endure the discovery that you know less than you thought. Ask the question anyway.
The embarrassment of being a beginner passes. But the cost of pretending you already know keeps growing.
It's thus much better to be a man of value than well-connected, but best to be both.
Keep learning. Work on your weaknesses. Refine your craft. Aim for excellence. Be genuine in helping others with problems aligning with your expertise.
You can take an attempt seriously without making its initial outcome a judgment on your entire future. There is still another version to make. Another rep. And another idea to try.

You can allow people to discover your abilities over time. A thoughtful observation, a problem handled well, or an unexpected skill often leaves a stronger impression than a prattled catalogue of achievements.
Success in persuasion requires knowing what moves each person. Common needs are ease, status, pleasure, and money but mostly connection and a good time.
Focusing on many goals disperses the potential of doing one well. It's thus wise to try one thing before moving on to another.

t: You’ve Got This
q: And when I reflect on our shoe tying lessons, I realize the real lesson wasn’t how to tie a shoe. It was how to care about someone enough to patiently work with them through their challenges without getting frustrated or giving up.
But sometimes caring for someone means doing something much harder; it means letting them struggle.

I think there’s a lot of wisdom packed into that idea, because caring and controlling can look remarkably similar, and if we’re not careful, we start making decisions for someone simply because we believe we know what’s best for them.
But our job isn’t to create little versions of ourselves; it’s to help our kids become capable of becoming themselves.
Protecting a child from every struggle may make childhood easier, but it won’t make adulthood better.
You may be surprised by what happens when you don’t immediately provide the answer. Sometimes they’ll make a mistake. Let them do that a lot when the stakes are low.

t: Why Preparation Is So Important for Decisions Involving Significant Risk
q: That conclusion misreads what preparation is for. Preparation doesn’t eliminate risk. It makes risk bearable.
Leaders can’t simply borrow confidence from past wins. They build it through preparation for the specific challenge in front of them.
When people imagine an outcome has already happened, they become markedly better at identifying the reasons it might occur.
As a result, prepared leaders step into uncertainty with conviction, not because they know how events will unfold, but because they trust their ability to navigate whatever does.
A leader who has studied the terrain, rehearsed the setbacks, and decided in advance how to respond is no longer held back by fear of what might go wrong.
Preparation isn’t playing it safe. It’s the license to play more boldly. The leaders who seem fearless rarely are. They are simply more prepared than others.
x: Preparation does not eliminate risk, the piece says, but it makes risk bearable by building earned confidence, which psychologists call self-efficacy.
Self-efficacy is challenge-specific, so confidence from past wins does not transfer and has to be rebuilt through preparation for each new challenge.
The note then draws on prospective hindsight, the finding that imagining an outcome as already having happened makes people better at identifying its causes and more accepting of the risk.
Apparent fearlessness is usually the visible result of unseen preparation, which is why prepared leaders can move while others hesitate.

t: When Training Becomes a Catch-All for Something Else
q: Training is a comfortable mental model. It’s also a tangible solution. You can build a course, schedule a webinar, create a guide, and check a box.

A process isn’t working, so we need training. A new system is launching, so we need training. People don’t know where to find information, so we need training. Expectations are inconsistent, so we need training.
But being able to contribute to something isn’t the same as being the right function to own it. There are questions of expertise. There are questions of authority.
We identify something a team can do and then this turns into something the team should do. But there’s a difference between competence and capacity.

Naming all of this “training” can overshadow the many resources necessary to solve the issue at hand. Because when we don’t see the full scope of the work, we’re much more likely to underestimate the time, expertise, people, and cross-functional coordination required to do it effectively.
And sometimes the most valuable thing a learning professional can do is recognize that the problem in front of us isn’t actually a learning problem at all.
Organizations get better outcomes when they diagnose the problem first and then determine the right intervention, expertise, ownership, and resourcing.
x: Because training is a comfortable, tangible solution that lets a team build a course and check a box, leaders reach for it before diagnosing what actually needs to change.
Melissa Muth Martinez argues that organizations use the word training as shorthand for a much broader set of needs, from process problems to new systems to unclear expectations.

A learning team may be competent to contribute to all of these, but she distinguishes competence from capacity and authority, since the ability to do something does not make a team the right owner or mean it is resourced for it.

Calling every organizational problem a training need hides the real scope of the work and leads to underestimating the time, expertise and coordination required.
A simple diagnostic sorts problems by what people know and can do, which points to a learning, process, technology, ownership, alignment or strategy response.

t: What to Say When You’re Challenged in Public
q: The calm leader was rated 4.92 out of seven for effectiveness. The leader who snapped and frowned scored 3.55. The leader who yelled and stomped scored 3.89.
Shouting gets noticed, and usually someone deals with it. The snap gets missed, most of all by the person doing it, because it feels like being firm.
The rules apply to one sentence only: the first thing you say after someone challenges you in front of others. Everything after it is easier if that one goes well.
Your voice is the first thing to go under pressure: the pitch rises and the pace picks up before you have decided anything. Lowering your voice is something you can do before you feel calm.
Hiding your reaction keeps it from others without making you any calmer.
My sense is that we snap downwards and over-explain upwards. Challenged by someone senior, the instinct is to defend every number at length, which is the same loss of composure, only more polite.
It does not feel like losing composure, which is why it goes unnoticed. To the person on the receiving end, it is the same snap spread over two weeks.
x: Snapping and frowning costs a leader nearly as much perceived effectiveness as shouting does, and the snap is harder to notice because it feels like firmness.
Snapping and frowning costs a leader nearly as much perceived effectiveness as shouting does, and the snap is harder to notice because it feels like firmness.
The four rules apply only to the first sentence after a challenge.
Ian Hallett opens with Elon Musk's dismissal of analysts' questions on a 2018 Tesla earnings call, which turned a capital question into a story about manners.
Hiding a reaction does not reduce arousal, so pair the visible rules with an internal reframe such as 'they are testing the plan, that is their job'.

t: True and Specific
q: The first principle of personal branding is this: You can’t build a personal brand. You can only control the initial conditions that shape what people believe about you…the work you do, how you do it and what you say no to.

But people also pay attention to how you do things. They notice what you say no to, how you treat people, and whether you live up to your values, keep your word, and follow through on the small stuff.

If everything you write sounds like everyone else, the people reading it will assume you’re like everyone else. If you say you believe something and do the opposite, people will assume you don’t truly believe it.
True means it matches who you are and reflects the true caliber of your work. If people believe less than what’s there, you get smaller opportunities than you deserve.
That’s how a brand turns into leverage: people say yes to your next thing before they’ve seen it.
If what they say could describe thousands of other people, like “a great consultant,” or if it sells your work short, posting more won’t fix that.
x: A personal brand is the belief people hold about you, and you can only shape it through your work, your refusals and how you treat people.
A personal brand is the belief people hold about you, and you can only shape it through your work, your refusals and how you treat people.

Josue Valles argues that personal branding is not posting on social media but shaping what other people believe about you, which you control only indirectly through the work you do, how you do it and what you say no to.
A brand works when it is true, which prevents both undersold opportunities and collapse under scrutiny, and specific, which separates you from thousands of peers.

His practical advice is to ask a few people who know your work how they would describe you to a friend and, if the answer is generic or undersells you, fix it through the work you take on before posting more.

t: The Untold Story of Bloom's Taxonomy and the Pyramid That Never Was
q: What they produced, in 1956, was a slim handbook for sorting test questions into six categories, arranged from the simplest demand on a student to the most complex. It was essentially a tool written by examiners for examiners.

There was no mention of a pyramid, and although the categories were arranged in order of increasing complexity, the committee was considerably more cautious about the significance of this ordering than the modern pyramid we all know would suggest.
The extraordinary thing about the pyramid is that nobody actually knows where it came from. It appears in neither the original 1956 handbook nor the revised taxonomy published in 2001.
To suggest that evaluating an argument depends on knowledge and understanding is one thing; to conclude that teaching this knowledge is therefore an inferior educational activity is quite another.

For me, there are two unfortunate ironies about Bloom’s taxonomy. The first is that a framework originally designed to help examiners think more precisely about educational objectives, has ironically encouraged teachers to think in a very imprecise way about learning.
He called it a problem, not a result: the question was how a class of thirty could get anywhere near it, and his own best answer was mastery learning.

Mastery learning was based on the claim that most of the variation in school achievement is created by schools themselves, more specifically by moving pupils on before they have learned what the next thing depends on, and that that can be remedied by a more accurate evaluation of what kids can know and do.
x: Carl Hendrick traces how Benjamin Bloom's 1956 taxonomy, a classification scheme written by examiners to compare test items, turned into a ranked pyramid that devalues knowledge.
No one knows who drew the pyramid, and it is absent from both the 1956 and 2001 publications, which makes it a later folk addition.
He shows that the original handbook described a neutral, descriptive scheme, likened to shelving books in a library, and that the pyramid appears in neither the 1956 nor the 2001 version.

Putting knowledge at the base slid from 'foundational' to 'lesser', encouraging objectives like 'think critically' with no specified knowledge to think with.
Bloom's 2 Sigma result was a problem to solve, not proof that tutoring is the ideal, and his answer for a class of thirty was mastery learning.
Mastery learning, with sequenced prerequisites and no moving on until they are secure, is Bloom's lasting contribution and the idea AI tutoring may finally make workable.

t: The Stories We Tell: Curriculum Design
q: If we want colleagues to understand and remember our message in order to influence their behaviour, telling stories appears an effective way of doing so.

Perhaps all would benefit from subject leaders harnessing the power of story to build collective knowledge of their subject, using the common features of stories: conflict, causality and complications.
The importance of conflict here is that that subject leaders can bring to life the interesting decisions that they have made and justify the reasoning.
No unit is an island and each must build on what has already been learned and lay the foundations for future learning – this is the essence of a coherent curriculum.
We then provide enough interaction for them to learn it as opposed to filling a unit of work with a number of lessons. If children need more time, we make it. If they need less, we can move on.

But there is a fourth ‘c’: character. Great stories have interesting characters and our curriculum is only as good as the impact it has on children. Children are the protagonists in our curriculum stories.
Great story telling is rooted in the knowledge of the story so subject leaders need to know an awful lot to be able to do this well.
x: In this installment of his Stories We Tell series, Nick Hart argues that subject leaders can use the structure of good stories, conflict, causality and complications, to help colleagues understand and remember curriculum intent.

Conflict in a curriculum story is the deliberate content choice, and 'we have always done it' or 'it is in the scheme' is not a reason a leader can tell a story about.
Causality appears in progression, where no unit is an island and concepts such as chronology or locational knowledge build year by year.
The lesson or the term is the wrong unit of time, because a curriculum built around a small amount of essential knowledge can flex to the time children need.

t: Small Moves That Help When Things Get Challenging
q: One of the overwhelming parts of teaching is the constant straddling of being present with students all day and still navigating the various other responsibilities of the job—many of which show up in our world through digital can-show-up-out-of-nowhere messages that are just a click away.
The value of waiting to open it is rather straightforward: it allows you to stay present within the classroom with students that is a win for them just as much as it is a win for you.

Sometimes we do not have agency over the stressful or frustrating aspects of our work, but I do believe we have agency over how we continue to lean into what is good—including how we name and invest in the good we are seeing around us.

I recognize that all this accumulated good can become its own obstacle, though, when the label of “good and meaningful” prevents us from honestly assessing our capacity and removing something from our plates when necessary.

There are many types of burnout as a teacher, but I think the most pernicious is when you start losing grasp of what actually matters to you in this work—and for me the best way to hold myself accountable to my own values is to make them as visible as possible
Slowing down to respond to a difficult email does not eliminate the difficult email, not to mention that it isn’t necessarily the best habit to be consistently delaying email responses.
x: Delay opening and answering non-urgent negative messages so the weight does not enter the classroom and your presence with students is protected.

Counterbalance a stressful interaction with a deliberate investment in something good, such as a positive note to a parent or celebrating a colleague.
Being good and meaningful is not enough to keep something on your plate.
Making core values visible, even listing each student's top value on the roster, keeps a teacher aligned and invites students to hold you accountable.

t: Small Children, Big Ideas
q: Her starting point was refreshingly straightforward: take a book, consider what it offers, and try something worthwhile with existing geography planning rather than inventing an entire unit from scratch.
The subject content remained uncompromisingly ambitious. What shifted was the means of access, captured through photographs and verbatim dialogue rather than completing a worksheet.
Participation means having something genuine to contribute that is recognised as worthwhile by the community of the classroom.
A copied sentence or coloured-in sheet shows task completion, but it tells us very little about what a child understands.
Saying “we made a map” describes an activity; explaining the features of that map begins to show geographical thinking.
True inclusion is never about watering down the curriculum. Vicky’s work points to a much better question: what might this subject make possible for this child?

t: Managing Cognitive Load with Mini-Whiteboards
q: Rather than putting an entire complex task in front of students and asking them to navigate it independently, I can break the task into manageable steps, provide and remove the appropriate scaffolding for each step, and keep only the information students need at that moment in their working memory.

Most importantly, students are not simultaneously processing the entire procedure, remembering my explanation, deciding what to do next, monitoring whether they are doing it correctly, and producing an answer.

Students can see everything that they will eventually have to do, even when they are not yet ready to do it. Many students will work ahead, moving into later steps before they have fully understood the knowledge, thinking, or procedure on which those steps depend.

The visual reference does not replace the explanation. Both are necessary but it prevents essential information that students still need in their environment to attend to and select from to enter working memory from disappearing the moment I stop saying or showing it.

A completed handout is certainly visible and collectable, but it is often a poor proxy for learning itself. It tells us that students did something. It does not necessarily tell us what they understood, what they retrieved, what connections they made, what misconceptions they corrected, or whether they could perform the thinking independently.

The important point is that the scaffolding is attached to a particular working memory demand at a particular moment. Students receive support when and where they need it, use it to complete the current step, and then move forward rather than carrying every scaffold with them through the entire task.
The purpose of this entire mini-whiteboard approach is not to keep students dependent on scaffolds or to permanently divide complex tasks into smaller pieces.
x: Students who can see the whole handout often work ahead before understanding the earlier step, producing predictable errors from overloaded working memory.
Projecting reference material such as a pattern table keeps transient explanation available while students apply it to their own examples.
Students who can see the whole handout often work ahead before understanding the earlier step, producing predictable errors from overloaded working memory.
A completed handout shows that students did something, not what they understood, so permanent artifacts should be reserved for work students will need to revisit.

Scaffolding is attached to a specific working-memory demand and then faded, moving students from highly supported execution toward independent coordination of the whole process.

t: Lesson Pace: Reducing Friction in Classrooms
q: When I personally think about pace, I tend to think about lessons not being rushed, but instead being sharp. After all, we don’t want rushed lessons or learning.
A well-paced classroom, therefore, is not necessarily one where tasks are moving quickly from one to the next like a train that rumbles on. It is, instead, one where very little gets in the way.
The aim isn’t achieving zero friction. It is trying to reduce friction as much as possible.
Familiarity is a key to pace. If children are unfamiliar with the routines and expectations, or how to participate within a lesson, we are allowing for unnecessary friction.

Frequently used resources need clear and explicit homes. Pupils need to know how to access these resources, replace them if they are no longer working, and how to put them away so that they’re ready to access again the next time they are needed.
Time is an abstract concept. Without a visible reference point, pupils can struggle to judge how quickly they need to work or how much time remains.

Missing a whiteboard pen is not desirable. Giving children an extra minute to retrieve previously learned knowledge and really unpick and wrestle with some key concepts and ideas, or to reconsider an incorrect answer, is a desirable difficulty we want to encourage.
x: Pace means a lesson with very little in the way, not a rushed one, so the goal is to reduce unnecessary friction rather than to talk or work faster.

Taught and rehearsed routines such as Show Me, cold calling and Turn and Talk free working memory because pupils no longer have to work out how to participate.

t: How Reacting Emotionally Can Ruin Your Authority
q: One of the biggest mistakes a teacher can make is to have an emotional reaction to misbehavior.
Like it or not, if your mood and behavior can be swayed by misbehavior, it communicates to your students that you’re not a strong leader.
Even the youngest students can recognize that outward signs of inner fragility prove that they can get under your skin and knock you off your center.
Lowering yourself to a misbehaving student’s level by battling with them or showing how they hurt your feelings makes you appear petty.
You promised to follow your classroom management plan as written. Period. If you lecture or admonish instead, or even in addition to, you’re going back on your word.
The solution is to allow your classroom management plan to do your dirty work for you. Let it handle all misbehavior.
In time and with consistency, the urge to react will go away. The result is that your authority will rise and your students will view you as a leader worth following.
x: Emotional loss of control makes the teacher less likable, and students follow leaders they admire.
Emotional loss of control makes the teacher less likable, and students follow leaders they admire.
He says this ruins authority for four reasons: it is weak, because students see that their behavior can knock the teacher off center.
Battling with a misbehaving student lowers the teacher to the student's level and reads as petty rather than strong.
Lecturing or admonishing in addition to the planned consequence breaks the promise to follow the plan as written, and inconsistency increases bad behavior and resentment.
The remedy is to let the management plan handle all misbehavior so the teacher's only job is consistent follow-through.
The teacher's only job is to follow it, and in time the urge to react fades while authority and student respect grow.

t: Disciplinary Knowledge 7 Years On
q: In 2019 school inspection in England shifted, making the curriculum the unit of inspection. For me and many others, the expectation of curriculum design changed almost overnight, prompting a re-examination of the national curriculum.

Curriculum narrowing was a significant finding of the inspections that led to the 2019 framework, as schools prioritised English and maths. The new framework looked at the foundation subjects in the same depth as the core.

First came the curriculum journey, and many leaders realised for the first time how incoherent their offer was: units repeated in different year groups, little material difference in expectations between years, and huge gaps between what was planned and what was taught (we ran out of time), let alone what was actually learned.

History became the flagship primary foundation subject and it was easy to see why. Disciplinary knowledge was clear and it took one article or one lecture from someone like Counsell to inspire a redesign and to do it well.

The high of history curriculum design wasn’t replicated in other subjects because the way of thinking about history didn’t quite fit. Every subject has slight variations in its logic and so the other foundation subjects weren’t as cleanly reinvigorated.
Ask the same question of a musician, a linguist or a writer, and much of the answer is about what they make, perform or say and how, rather than how they establish claims.
If a definition works beautifully in one subject but not others, there are two possible explanations. Either the other subjects haven’t done the work or the definition is too narrow.

t: Your Life Touches More Lives Than You Know
q: We can be fully responsible for our lives while recognizing that the quality of those lives is profoundly affected by one another.
We are an extraordinarily interconnected species, even though we sometimes like to imagine otherwise.
Do people generally leave an interaction with you a little more uplifted or a little more depleted? More seen or less seen? More capable, more hopeful, more themselves—or slightly diminished?

t: I Learned in a Due Process Hearing That the Accommodations Never Happened
q: I was thinking about a twelve-year-old who had spent seven months in rooms where the adults did not know what he needed, while his mother trusted the paper I had signed. A signature on a plan is not a plan in the classroom.

t: The Town Hall Is Broken and Leaders Know It
q: The gap between what organisations communicate and what employees actually believe is one of the most thoroughly documented and least acted-upon problems in organisational life. It has its own data, its own literature and it is getting worse.

The leaders designing the communications believe, with reasonable confidence, that their messaging is landing, believed and trusted. The people receiving it are, in significant numbers, not buying it.

The result is a communication system that is technically functioning (messages are being sent, received, and politely acknowledged) while culturally failing. The town hall happens but nothing changes.

If line managers are the most credible communication channel in most organisations, then the communication strategy that ignores them (that treats them as message carriers rather than conversation facilitators) is not just inefficient. It is actively undermining the most valuable trust asset the organisation has.

The standard response to the town hall’s inadequacy is to add more channels: the intranet article that nobody reads, the CEO video blog with a comment section that nobody uses, the pulse survey whose results are shared in aggregate six weeks later with no visible action. These are the town hall’s digital cousins; broadcast mechanisms dressed up as dialogue.

Genuine two-way communication (the kind that rebuilds trust rather than merely performing it) has structural requirements that most organisations find uncomfortable. It requires small groups, not large ones. It requires leaders who are genuinely willing to hear difficult things and be seen to act on them.

The solution is not a better communications strategy. It is leaders who are willing to say difficult things clearly, to acknowledge what they don’t know, and to treat the people they lead as capable of handling the truth.

t: 7 Presentation Habits for Experts Who Build the Slides First
q: I have coached over 300 speakers and run more than 30 events, and this is the most common structural error I see. The deck becomes the plan, and a deck is a poor plan, because it organises your material rather than the audience’s experience of it.
A room does not want a survey. They came with something specific they need, which may be two of your nine sections, and the other seven are costing you their attention while you deliver them.
Your opening buys the attention you spend in the middle. Nothing after it gets a fair hearing if those first sentences were spent on your name, your job title, and how pleased you are to be here.
Sentence two: where are they at the end? Not what you will have covered. What will have changed in them.
That gap is the entire talk. Anything that does not serve the move comes out, however good it is, and most of what you were planning to include does not serve it.
The rule is not that scripting fails, it is that half-memorising fails, because you end up fluent enough to recite and not fluent enough to be present.
Nobody has ever complained about a presentation that ended early, and finishing with ten minutes spare gives the room something they value more than your last three slides.
A slide earns its place by showing something your voice cannot. A trend, a photograph, a comparison that is genuinely visual.

One thing that helps is having a stock question to repeat over and over again. How do you know? How did you decide? If teachers ask the same question regardless of accuracy of the student’s answer, the students recognize that the words aren’t a hint.

t: We All Need Microadventures

A person does not need to consider themselves an adventurer to go on a microadventure; they simply have to leave their house and see what happens.

t: Silence Is Not How Science Advances: Roland Fryer's Call for Courage
q: Roland Fryer is clear and convincing when he says he’s interested in scientific truth, not ideological storytelling.

Fryer himself endured public condemnation—and physical threats—when he published his research about policing that stated findings contradicting the prevailing viewpoint, so he speaks from experience when he says he’s siding with science, not social acceptability.

Fryer deflates the commonly-held belief that poverty dooms educational success and that we can’t improve student outcomes until we’ve improved their societal circumstances. During his three years working with the Houston schools, they were able to close the achievement gap in math.

What is insidious about the belief that schools are powerless to overcome society’s ills is that it is not only used to excuse lack of student progress, but also to justify lack of pursuing educational change at every level based on current research.
Fryer showed us that solving the racial achievement gap is not predicated on solving poverty. It can be done by improving the quality of education.
Roland Fryer has exhibited—and now wants to reward—a different kind of courage, one that can threaten your livelihood and your safety, not just your peace of mind.

While it is true that knowing what research says is not the same thing as successfully translating that research into classroom practice, not knowing what it says doesn’t even provide us the opportunity for a translation to teaching.

t: Proof is the New Proof
q: AI has made ideas and even ability so cheap that the only real differentiator left is proof. And if you don’t have proof, you aren’t going to get reach.
Simply: Real people, solving real problems, and getting real results that other real people need.
So whoever did actually take the time to create content like the listicle would, almost by default, be considered an expert. This was true whether they actually did the things or not.

t: Invisible classrooms: What we’ve learned about education news since the Nikole Hannah-Jones essay
q: Classroom instruction is a fundamental mechanism for perpetuating or disrupting inequity. Schools and districts organize instruction — more by default than by design — so that some kids consistently get much more opportunity to learn than others.
In an 8,000-word essay about a child’s schooling, there is vivid description of poor teaching but little investigation of how it came to be and why it’s tolerated.

We have good evidence that there is more variation in the quality of instruction from class to class than from school to school — in other words, which teacher my kid gets matters more to their future outcomes than which school they go to.

t: Intuition Gets Stronger the More You Listen to It
q: Murakami did not want to become an employee of a conglomerate, a company, or any other organization. But he didn’t imagine himself leading one either.
For an instant, a life presents itself from an angle that had not been visible before. The view is striking.
Opening the jazz bar had required him to distinguish between the life he wanted for himself from the one that others expected of him.
Even if there was not material proof that he could make it as a novelist, Murakami sold the bar against the all too familiar objections of everyone around him.
By the time he gave up the bar, he was not relying on the same intuition he had possessed years earlier. It had been exercised by use.
Running it had taught him that conviction could survive contact with debt and fatigue.
None of these steps gave him certainty about the one that followed. The jazz bar didn’t contain proof of a literary career, and winning a prize didn’t mean that he would become a lasting novelist.
The confidence appeared after each act, not before it. Every intuition he carried into reality left him better able to recognize and trust the next.

t: How Prideful Is Your Team?
q: Pride comes from four primary sources: the quality of the work, the higher purpose or social value of the work, the history and reputation of the enterprise, and the skills and expertise of colleagues.
Leaders who emphasize performance and goal attainment without connecting those outcomes to one or more of the four sources limit the benefits of team pride.
When a project succeeds, they talk about the craftsmanship behind it, not just the number it hit. When the goal is set, they explain the higher purpose it will serve and why that matters socially.
Team pride is not arrogance. Prideful teams don’t look down on others or resist critical feedback. Instead, pride raises the standard a team holds for itself.
Research suggests prideful teams correct mistakes faster, defend their reputation through their behavior, and attract talented colleagues who want to belong to something admired.

t: Churchill and the Art of Persuasion
q: Of all the talents bestowed upon men, none is so precious as the gift of oratory. He who enjoys it wields a power more durable than that of a great king. He is an independent force in the world.

Importantly, he does not hide from the precarious situation of the Allies nor the difficult implications of what occurred at Dunkirk. Indeed, Churchill goes out of his way to prevent any premature sense of triumph, reminding Parliament that, “We must be very careful not to assign to this deliverance the attributes of a victory. Wars are not won by evacuations.

In his book Rhetoric, the fourth-century BC philosopher outlined three fundamental modes of persuasion: ethos, pathos, and logos. These are the character and credibility of the speaker, the emotions of the audience, and the argument itself.
Churchill does not tell Parliament they should believe him, he presents his trustworthiness instead by not concealing anything or trying to diminish the hardships they are facing.

q: Sometimes a bad academic study is just a bad academic study, particularly when its title is misleading. We should be able to admit that.

The problem is that the report does not produce what it promises. It does not directly measure course-integrated AI tutoring, and while it may have included randomization, the treatment group did not take the same drug (i.e., AI tutoring).
That sounds consequential, but what, exactly, produced those effects? Only about 15% of students offered access ever used the tool—and only 13% in the same-course sample.
Among students who tried it, the average was approximately four sessions. About 40% had only one session, while a few heavy users pulled up the average.

Answering a course question is not, by itself, tutoring. Tutoring should attempt to find out what a learner understands, diagnose misunderstandings, and adapt explanations, hints, and practice accordingly.
And that “integration” really just meant technical LTI integration with the LMS, not integration into teaching methods. Yet “AI tutoring” gets top billing in the title.

EdTech isn't like some learning grenade you toss into ignorance and when it explodes people learn. EdTech was never a passive change-maker. EdTech is a tool, and how that tool is/isn't used is EVERYTHING.
That is a finding EdTech needs: availability is not adoption, and adoption is not evidence of better learning. What students do with a tool—and how instructors integrate it—requires attention.

t: 1MW No. 326: What We Get Wrong About Staying in Touch
q: Connection is not built in grand gestures. It is built in small signals of care.
In her new book, Conversation, she turns this penguin ritual into a human practice called pebbling: small, thoughtful gestures that signal care.
Each one, she writes, carries the same message: "I noticed you. I remembered. I care.

In a 2023 study published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, researcher Peggy Liu and her colleagues found that people routinely underestimate how much a simple check-in message will be appreciated by the person receiving it.
Most of us hold back anyway. We assume our message is too small to matter, like it’s an interruption or noise that nobody wants to hear.
After a meaningful conversation, follow up within three days. For friends you rarely see, a small check-in every four to six weeks keeps the bond warm.
Pebbles don’t need to be a huge thing. Small is good. Small is caring.

t: 10 Lessons It Took Me 10 Years To Understand
q: The Stoics believed that the purpose of the philosophy was to make you a better person. Stoicism isn’t just about what it can do for you. It also asks a lot of you.
The “opportunity” the Stoics saw inside adversity, big and small, was the opportunity to practice virtue.

You want to make sure your discipline is not compulsion. That you have the strength to do the things that actually need to be done, and the discipline to say no to the things you shouldn’t do anymore.
Seneca defines this as a form of poverty. He says poverty is not just having too little. It’s also wanting more.

Epictetus talks about this most movingly, given the adversity he experienced: the key is to wish for things to go the way they have gone. To see them as uniquely fated and designed for you, because they have set you up to be who you are.
At 29, memento mori made me go faster. At 39, it reminds me: don’t rush this. Because what are you rushing towards?
Stoicism is an evolving thing. Your study and understanding of it is an evolving thing. It is not something you studied. It is something you are studying.
You don’t graduate from philosophy. You practice it. Even if you teach it, you remain a student.
x: Holiday's central correction is that Stoicism exists to make a person better and to serve the common good, not merely to make them tougher or more productive.
He recasts 'the obstacle is the way' as an opportunity to practice the four virtues, which makes even tragedy a place for character rather than a puzzle to be turned into advantage.

t: You Don’t Need Another AI-Generated Worksheet
q: Instead of asking AI to invent a lesson from scratch, we’re going to give it three precise jobs inside one saved conversation to generate a complete lesson sequence:
When I see teachers prompt their LLM with something like “make me an engaging lesson,” I see that it leaves almost every important decision to the chatbot while wondering why “AI isn’t that great.
A more useful prompting request begins with decisions you’ve already made: what students need to understand, what they will read, and how they will interact with it.
Wicked Hydra changes the intellectual job entirely. Instead of producing the right answer, students practice noticing what they don’t know yet and generating questions worth pursuing.
Across one class period, students move from retrieving knowledge to making meaning, then into curiosity, and finally back to retrieval with a stronger mental model than they started with.
CAUTION: Never give students the chatbot’s synthesis or takeaway summaries. If you hand them the big idea up front, you’ve quietly completed the most important part of the thinking for them.

And also, please don’t accidentally gaslight yourself into believing that a single set of prompts will fix an impossible workload. It wont, but it might keep one more piece of that workload from eating your Sunday.

t: You Are the Key: Never Ignore Your Self-Story
q: The stories we tell ourselves are incredibly powerful. We often accept narratives about ourselves which work against us.

I have found repeatedly that it is impossible to win enough hearts and minds by dealing with people’s beliefs. But as soon as success happens, because of the checklist, beliefs change. Checklist first, hearts and minds second.
We all have limiting beliefs imposed on us by our environment – by our experience of school. A checklist helps you override this – you follow it, even if your beliefs don’t match.

Understanding your self-story will help you understand both your potential – which is much greater than you think – and your limiting beliefs, which, for most of us – are even greater than we would like to admit.
Balance your aspirations with an accurate understanding of what is actually within your control, ensuring that your goals are grounded rather than mere wishful thinking.

t: Why Being Wrong Can Feel So Right
q: We interpret new information using what we already know. Our existing knowledge and experience help shape what we notice, how we understand it, and what we remember.
A “schema” is organized knowledge about a familiar kind of object, event, or situation, including relationships and expectations.
In this way, patterns give us a head start in adjusting to a new situation.
A key idea to remember: the mind is constantly trying to fit new information into what we already know.
So you turn the thermostat to the maximum setting, expecting it to heat faster. The context and your existing knowledge provided a plausible explanation that felt correct to you.
The problem was not the reality of thermostats, but expectations you brought to the table.

Everyone has patterns and expectations that are invisible. Part of clear communication is anticipating the audience’s assumptions (dials lead to faster heating) and finding ways to update their patterns.

q: Word problems require students to find solutions by applying their math skills, but first they must apply their literacy skills to understand what problem they have to solve. If they struggle with the latter, it may not matter how strong they are in math.
Parents often assume the problem lies in their children’s math skills and discount the role literacy skills play in solving word problems.

Helping students improve their ability to solve math word problems begins with improving their reading fluency.

t: What the Cornell Allegations Reveal About How America Raises Sons
q: What happened at Cornell is to be expected when success is defined by performance instead of moral virtue.
The truth is that these men arrived on campus with moral values already in place, and their fraternity provided a context for them to be the men they were raised to be.
As a society, we have purged religious formation as a concomitant framework necessary for true male success.
This is not about teaching men about consent. It’s about raising men to be virtuous, and that’s what our culture doesn’t care about today.
The “Cornell 7” is what happens when a culture raises young men to gain the world but does nothing to cultivate their souls.
We need to stop believing the myth that what makes a “good kid” a “good kid” is his résumé rather than his moral excellence.

These categories are useful. Sometimes they are necessary. But they are never the whole person.
When we see people one-dimensionally, it should not surprise us that we create one-dimensional responses.
Every system we create eventually lands in a human life. Every policy. Every organizational decision.

t: The Most Confident Person in the Room Is Usually the Most Afraid
q: He was not powerful. He was terrified. His vision could not survive contact with arithmetic, everyone was about to watch it happen, and the only move fear left him was to make the person holding the numbers sit down.
Each was afraid of being found out. Each had learned the safest place to hide fear is behind confidence, because nobody checks the person who seems sure.
Confidence and competence look exactly alike from the outside. In the few seconds it takes to form an impression of someone, there is no way to tell them apart.
When someone junior flinches, nothing happens. When the most powerful person in the building does, everyone below rearranges themselves around it, and the whole company starts softening the truth.
A frightened boss cannot stand the person who sees what he misses, so he takes the deck, kills the forecast, and tells the truth to sit down. The secure one keeps her close.
Fear wants agreement, because agreement never exposes it. Confidence can stand to be corrected.
Their fear becomes your fear, and you carry it long after they are gone.

t: The Default-Off Classroom: Redefining 1:1 Programs for Meaningful Learning
q: We are very good at explaining the logistics of a 1:1 program and very poor at explaining the learning, and families can tell the difference.
Walk into any 1:1 school and ask four people the same three questions: how is technology used here, why do students have devices, and at what age do they get them.

Screen time is an empty data set. A count of minutes with a device open cannot say what happened in those minutes, and the way it gets reported quietly supplies the answer anyway: every minute was the tool being used as intended.
When the lid is closed until a teacher opens it, the minutes stop being the question. The reason it was opened is the question, and whether the purpose was met is the data.
A school device is a tool among tools. Sometimes it is the right one. Sometimes the right tool is a pencil, a printed novel, a lab bench, a walk outside, or two students talking to each other.
People stay where you put them. The lid-up classroom is a default nobody chose, set by a cart, a login, and a pandemic. Resetting it is a decision, and it has to be made by two people at once.

t: Stop Confusing Montessori with Self-Directed Education
q: Montessori is a theory of the right conditions, built by an adult who has studied where a child should end up. Self-Directed Education is a theory of what children already do when nothing gets in the way.
The two approaches overlap in genuine ways, but they originate from two different beliefs about who a child already is.
Does a child need an adult to design the right environment for them, or does a child already have what they need to learn on their own?
A Montessori child chooses, but she chooses from options an adult has already decided are worth choosing. The environment itself functions as the curriculum.
Democracy decides what most children want. Sociocracy decides what works for every child in the room, which means a single child's objection carries real weight against the whole group.

But these are self-selected surveys, gathered from families who already believe in the model enough to choose it and stay with it. There is no randomized study of Self-Directed Education comparable to the lottery-based Montessori research.

t: Reverse-Audience Building
q: An audience doesn’t automatically give you clients or referrals or a spot on a big stage. An audience is a proxy for reputation.
So you might get the big number and still not get the clients, the referrals or the invitations to speak.
Write down a list of 30, 40, or 50 people you deeply admire, you’d love working with, or who could open a door for you. Then, start creating just for them.
I call this “reverse-audience” building because you’re building your audience before you publish anything.
The idea is that you give them a reason to get to know you, without asking them for anything.
Your follower count barely moves while you’re working one person at a time. But the point was always the opportunities, and opportunities come from people.
Plus, AI is making content abundant, so this type of content becomes more valuable every year.

t: Live with Uncertainty
q: That kind of knowledge exists only about things that are finished. You can be certain about last year because last year is over.
Staying where you are is also a choice, and its outcome is just as hidden. The job you keep, the conversation you put off, and the idea you leave in a drawer all lead somewhere you cannot see either.
So the useful question before a decision is whether you have good reasons, and that one can be answered today. Write down what you know, what you want, and the worst realistic result.
So every shot has two parts. The shot itself belongs to him. Where the arrow lands belongs to him only partly.

An archer who is thinking about the prize, or about how a miss will look to the crowd, has less attention left for his hands. Fear of the result makes the shot worse.
