t: Learning Is a Purchase. Adoption Is a Practice.
q: Learning is a purchase. Adoption is a practice. They happen in different places, at different times, and only one of them is for sale.
A meta-analysis of 47 experiments found that when an intervention produced a strong change in intention, behavior moved about half as far.
The strongest factor was not insight or motivation. It was repetition in a consistent context.
Predictable lowers the threat of trying something new. Consistent makes the practice worth repeating. Kind makes the first clumsy attempt survivable.

t: You Can't Think Clearly in a Room Full of Noise
q: It took me a long time to realize the problem was never a lack of information. It was too much noise, and no quiet place to actually think inside of.
Thinking is not the same thing as consuming information. Thinking is what happens after you stop consuming, when you actually sit with what you’ve taken in and let it settle into something usable.
A mind that is constantly reacting to input has no room left to evaluate it. You cannot judge something clearly while you’re still being hit by it.
You’re not stupid. You’re just depleted, and depletion looks a lot like confusion from the inside.
Silence, on purpose, before you decide anything that matters. Not silence as an escape. Silence as a workspace.
The people who seem to make good decisions quickly aren’t smarter. They’ve just built the habit of thinking before they consume, instead of consuming until a decision falls out by accident.
Most of the time, you’ll find you haven’t really thought at all. You’ve just been absorbing.

t: Working With Parents Who Only Value Top Achievement For Their Child
q: I’ve seen students who have worked very hard, and who have achieved really good results, only to be met with a parent’s disappointment.

What parents often don’t realise is that this kind of pressure can create fear and perfectionism, and can lead to their child believing that nothing they do can ever enough. And that mindset often leads to worse performance on future tests.
When I come across this, I don’t try to win the argument. I’ve learned that pushing too hard only makes parents dig their heels in and stick to their position more.
I’ve found that if I’m specific about where I praise a student’s work, it usually feels more credible to parents who value measurable achievement.
Some parents believe that if their child struggles, something is wrong, so I point out that the topic being studied is often challenging for most students.

I help students to separate their identity from their grades by reminding them that they are not their score, and a grade only measures their performance on one day. It can never measure their intelligence or their worth, but sadly this is a message they rarely hear at home.

I’m aware of when the healthiest thing to do is to stop trying to convince the parent about why top grades don’t fully show the progress a student has made. I’ve learned to state my case once, clearly, and then let it rest.

stop watching hours, start watching output only. If the work gets done and nothing breaks, the day is theirs to shape.

q: A team at Ambition Institute pooled 56 randomised experiments, all run in real schools, to test whether adding visuals such as pictures and diagrams to spoken or written explanations helps pupils learn.

q: But when fear overwhelms us, preoccupation with the future can become a trap. And in trying to protect our children, we may find we’ve forfeited their childhood.

t: If Marriages Are Lasting Longer, How Can We Make Them Last for Life?
q: Marriages may be lasting longer, but longevity alone is no cause for celebration. The end of a marriage is not simply a private affair between two adults. Its consequences reach far beyond the home and into society itself.

Since the introduction of no-fault divorce in the UK in 2022, ending a marriage has become easier than ever. You can initiate a divorce from your iPhone on your commute to work, using the Government’s online platform to initiate the process, without speaking to another person.
The average cost of couples counselling is £80 per session, putting it out of reach for many whose marital difficulties already center on finances.
Supporting marriage does not mean that every couple should stay together. No one should be forced to remain in a relationship that is dangerous or harmful.

Marriage has become increasingly secularized: a civil contract with a get-out clause and, for some, a mere token Instagram display. For marriage to survive every season of life, it must be rooted in something deeper.

There are two failure modes from here. Absolute dismissal costs you the signal. Rumination costs you hours of attention you did not budget for.
Treat feedback you disagree with like a suspect bug report. Do not shut the door on it immediately.
Set a time box. This takes self-control, but saves you time in waffling on the actions to take and the thoughts replaying.
You can paste the feedback directly into your favorite AI LLM and ask: What are three interpretations of this, so I don’t assume bad intent?
You are not outsourcing your judgment. You own your human judgment. But you are giving yourself another angle to consider.
As for your go-forward decision at the end of the time window and when more clarity is reached, it is your decision: adopt, adapt, or respectfully decline.
The worst outcome isn’t unfair feedback itself; it’s when it never gets resolved in your own mind.

t: History that Nourishes the Soul
q: The first stereotype I might call the Droning Lecturer—the antiquarian who focuses on the minutiae of historical detritus, and fails to help students perceive the whole.
When we recognize history for what it is—a limited kind of knowledge that invites the application of rhetoric as we explore what it means to be human—studying and teaching history renews our souls.
The student of history’s goal is not judgment, but understanding.

Rather than “Why did the Crusaders commit moral atrocities?” (which is an excellent question for an ethics course), the student of history asks “Why did the Crusaders believe these moral atrocities were the right course of action?
Rather than a disconnected present, the historically conscious individual sees himself as connected to the persons of both past and future
The historian begins with the remnants, and attempts to reconstruct the whole world within which the fragments existed. Such a construction is always limited, and subject to change.
History thus becomes an application of rhetoric - the use of all available means of persuasion, to answer a question as truly as possible.
The study of history operates rather like the description of a will - by studying history, you learn what you have inherited. What you make of that inheritance is up to you.

t: Epicurus - Proto-Scientist, Secular-Saint, and Sophisticated Hedonist
q: There is probably no other ancient Greek philosopher who has been so misunderstood in our modern era. Nowadays his philosophy is associated with excess and drinking and food apps… but the reality is, he preached the exact opposite.
He utilized his garden as a classroom, and relied heavily on donations to survive. Aside from the occasional college party, Epicurus and his students lived mostly on bread and water.

Epicurus developed his philosophy with a practical aim in mind, and so employed the use of logic and rationality as a means to happiness, rather than as tools for uncovering the truth for truth’s sake.
Although Epicurus outlines a hedonistic ethic, it is a sophisticated theory that encourages moderation.
Just as important to the Epicurean ethic is a reduction of desires. If we want less, we will be happy with less.
Friendship was the highest human relationship for Epicurus because it provided security, tranquility, and pleasure.
Furthermore, he argued that death is nothing to be fearful about, because it does not concern us.
Imagine the eternity before your birth… the eternity of nothingness. That doesn’t seem scary; you didn’t experience that nothingness.

t: Criticism From a Leader Who Doesn't Believe in You
q: The team member doesn’t hear, “This is the way to get better.” Instead, they hear “This is more evidence that you don’t belong.
Softening the criticism doesn’t solve the problem because muted praise signals low expectations just as clearly as harsh words do.

Before offering critical feedback, good leaders state plainly why they are giving it. “I’m pointing these things out because the bar is high and I’m confident you can meet it.” This short statement changes the meaning of everything that follows.
When leaders don’t believe, they leak doubt in small behaviors, such as who gets coveted assignments, who gets interrupted, whose ideas get credited, and who gets attention during performance.
Leaders don’t owe everyone their belief, but they do owe everyone the truth about whether they have it.
A slow exit dressed up as development and support is still an exit, only crueler.
Figure out how to believe in people or tell them the truth. Anything in between is just a polite surrender.

t: Atomization in Early Elementary Science
q: Atomization is a term used by some to describe the process of decomposing materials into the smallest necessary units, and ensuring that each new atom is explicitly taught one at a time.

A central principle here is that, in line with cognitive load theory, students should be presented with one new concept, or atom, at a time. Students should gain mastery over each atom before building upon it.
However, focusing on multiple items at once violates the “one new concept at a time" rule that cognitive load demands.
For example, kindergartners know dogs, cats, and elephants are animals, but they often do not know that bugs or people are animals.

It is precisely because we break down the content into manageable pieces that students are able to understand complex concepts and build the foundational knowledge that is essential to higher-order thinking.
Students who come to school with high background knowledge can often get by with curriculum that skips explicitly teaching the foundations. Students without this privilege get left behind
If you want to talk about gap-closing, if you want to talk about equity, then talk about explicit instruction and atomization.

Teachers should not be the ones responsible for atomizing their entire year of content — it’s a time-intensive process. This should be the purview of curriculum developers who ideally provide options for differentiation.

t: A Museum Teaches Us to Move Through Complexity Without Seeing Everything All at Once
q: Museums are a perfect model for understanding complex work because they give you enough orientation to make the next move in the environment. You learn the museum and art by moving through it.
But it confuses information with clarity. It can create information overload when actually what’s needed is more clarity for better decisions.

If we want to know the whole, we want comprehension. If we need to know enough about where we are today, the current surroundings (dependencies), and what the next moves should be, then we want orientation.
Signage at each junction does more for viewing than a paper guide handed to visitors at the entrance.
A project plan is a partial view of the project. A dashboard shows the parts someone chose to measure, and an org chart doesn’t show who people go to when something breaks.
In museums, visitors follow the chronology, wander to bright rooms, follow their favorite artist, or sit for hours looking at a single painting. Nothing is dictated, everything designed.
I’m not saying museums prove how organizations should run complex work. They don’t. Research tells us how people move through exhibition spaces.

t: A Guide to Listening Well (to Audiobooks)
q: Another way I have used Audiobooks is as a tool for prereading the books that I already knew I wanted to engage with deeply as a physical book. By ‘prereading’ I mean a kind of superficial read where you work through the book to gain an introductory familiarity with its structure, terms content and, in the case of fiction, plot.

To do this, I would take any book I may be interested in reading and begin listening to it, specifically with the intent of determining whether or not it was a book I should put on the more limited list of books I could sit down and read in the near future.
One of my favorite uses for Audiobooks is pairing, which is where I strategically pair an audiobook with a physical book that I am reading.

I have found that occasionally referencing the table of contents and dipping in to read the beginning or end of a chapter here and there increases my “reading” (listening?) comprehension and retention.

A second tip, which works especially well if you are listening while driving alone, is to pause the audiobook occasionally and to discuss it out loud to yourself. Give yourself some time to think about and engage with what you’ve just listened to instead of listening continuously without breaks.

Lastly, I recommend using the bookmark feature found in most audiobook apps, like Libro.fm and Audible to capture important clips, favorite quotes or sections of the book you want to revisit to think more about later.
If you are someone who thinks of reading as a special, formative practice, and would like to get the most out of your audiobooks, this is for you.

t: You Can Lead Change. You Can't Force Teachers to Own It.
q: What we file as resistance is usually people protecting something that still works.

The department head who ignored the policy was not being insubordinate, she had done a sum the leadership never did, and what the audit logged as non-compliance was a workload alarm going off in the only language available to it.

Keep the first and let the second go. Maths meets the standard with live marking under a visualiser and a coded key; English with fewer, longer written responses; somebody else records voice notes on the bus home.

A change is not owned while it still lives in the leader’s vocabulary. If the head is still saying “our formative feedback framework” and the science team, in the prep room, call it “closing the loop” and have built their own five-minute routine to do it, the change has left the office.
A new approach rarely asks a teacher only to learn something. It asks her to accept that the way she did it for twenty years was, in some measure, wrong.
Understanding, ownership and adoption are three different events. You can see why a thing must change. You can make it yours. You can still decline to do it.

What a leader controls is the invitation, the conditions, the design, the quality of the listening, whether the system can genuinely bend. What a leader does not control is another adult’s final decision.

t: Yes, Writing Does Advance Thinking
q: But writing is more powerful because it’s harder. It requires more precision and clarity.
Writing also serves as a visible record of our thinking. That means that when our ideas are incoherent or fragmentary, writing makes those problems more obvious.

The big caveat is that the task of writing itself is extremely cognitively demanding. If students are overwhelmed by the cognitive load of writing, they won’t have the capacity to get the learning benefits writing can bring.
In fact, evidence from cognitive science establishes that learning and thinking are inextricably linked: the more we learn about a topic, the better able we are to think critically about it.

q: Belonging says I have a place here. Mattering has two sides, feeling valued and adding value, and it asks a harder question: would this room be different if I weren’t in it?

t: When to stop coaching an underperformer
q: You stop. You stop whether the problem is the coach or the coachee and whether the coachee can’t change or won’t change.

t: What is going on in education in England?
q: The big global headline was that the OECD average scores on maths and reading were the lowest ever recorded in the history of the tests. And a very significant sub-plot is that England is one of the very few countries to have resisted this downward trend.

But whilst England’s scores have held steady, Scotland and Wales have declined sharply. 15-year-olds in England used to be behind those in Scotland. They are now about a year ahead in maths and science, and ahead by a smaller amount in reading.

In short, PISA is a screen-based test of problem-solving skills that requires limited specific curriculum knowledge. If you wanted to design a test that would be least likely to reward England’s educational approach, and most likely to reward the approach in Scotland & Wales, it would be PISA.

We are now in the situation where the statistics and the underlying science are pointing in the same direction. England adopted an approach to education explicitly influenced by Hirsch and insights from cognitive science. It is now outperforming many countries on international educational surveys.

And to improve education, we could gain a lot just by doing better at spreading existing best practice. That is to say, even without any big new scientific breakthroughs, we could still improve just by making effective teaching methods more widely used.
The whole world is worrying about their kids getting dumber. England appear to have the policy solution. And yet the government in England seem to want to reverse those policies.
x: Daisy Christodoulou reviews the 2025 PISA results for an international readership and argues that England has resisted a global decline in reading and maths scores.
England's relative PISA success is presented as a natural experiment, since England, Scotland and Wales diverged after 2010 and only the knowledge-focused system held its scores.

She answers the objection that PISA may be unreliable by noting that PISA is itself a progressive, problem-solving test that should favour Scotland and Wales, and that England also does well on TIMSS and PIRLS.
Following Hirsch, she says two kinds of evidence are needed, outcome statistics and cognitive science, and that for England both now agree.

Her practical proposal is to spread existing best practice, for example by training a cadre of 100 leaders from successful schools to lead 100 struggling ones, rather than wait for a scientific breakthrough.
She flags a policy paradox: other countries are asking to learn from England just as its government plans to reverse the reforms.

t: What I Learned the Year I Let Kids Fail
q: What I was doing, I finally realized, was managing behavior. I wasn’t teaching responsibility.

Managing behavior means the teacher carries the weight of the consequence — you track it, you enforce it, you decide when it’s resolved. Teaching responsibility means the consequence belongs to the student.
A zero isn’t a punishment in my room — it’s a record of what happened, and it stays unless the student does something about it.
By April, he was one of my most reliable students. Not because I fixed him — because I stopped removing the conditions that were supposed to motivate him to fix himself.
I stopped asking “why didn’t you do this?” and started asking “what’s your plan?” The first question is about the past.
I’d separated my effort from their result, which is where it should have been separated all along.
once he understood I wasn’t going to catch him when he fell, he started watching where he was stepping.

What frightens me instead is that the vast majority of educators do not have the slightest idea that the latest advances in AI are pulling the rug out from under their feet. We therefore desperately need more AI literacy among educators.

t: Does Teacher Expertise Matter?

q: Great teaching isn’t accidental, mystical, or reducible to charisma or other personality traits. It’s built on knowledge, judgment, and years of deliberately working on the gradual development of expertise.
Experience isn’t enough, it’s necessary but insufficient on its own. We often confuse experience with expertise, but they aren’t the same.
Expertise isn’t just accumulated time and speed/routine. It’s organised, refined, and reflected-upon experience.
Expert teachers don’t simply do the basics better. They see more, notice more, infer more, and respond more precisely.
The second is pattern recognition. Expert teachers are better at seeing what’s going on because they have better organised knowledge structures (i.e., cognitive schemata) in their long-term memory.
The fourth is deliberate practice. Expertise doesn’t develop through experience alone. It develops when teachers work consciously on getting better at specific aspects of practice.

t: Climbing On Autopilot
q: Because we tend to have a career story ready, but we less often have a clear reason why our career has gone that way.

Most career advice is about acceleration and continuous progress: how to get promoted faster, and how to close the distance between where you are and where you want to be. But that framing doesn’t examine what “getting there” actually costs.
The reason we keep deferring our desires is that career progress has a price tag attached. You can put a number on what you’d lose by stepping sideways or slowing down.
The result is a system where capable people conclude, again and again, that they can’t afford to do the things they’re working so hard to eventually afford.
That persistence is itself evidence. If the climbing were really about arriving, arriving would be enough to stop it.

Between the two effects, the leader is squeezed from both directions: the organisation keeps raising what it expects, and the leader’s own sense of achievement keeps requiring more to register at all.
A promotion decision is almost always a readiness check (can this person do the job?), and tends to miss the motive check asking whether that person should want the job, and why.
So you should re-justify the climb to yourself at every rung. Your manager can ask the question, and a good organisation can make space for it, but the thinking is yours alone.

t: When Math Stops Being the Measure of Intelligence

If the top priority received the fewest hours, you have found the gap. Then move hours to it, or change the ranking.
Supervision means the team has to ask you where things stand. In the handovers above, the owners keep the record, and you read it, and the team can see its own progress.
Put one question to your leadership team at its next meeting: “If someone read our calendars and budgets for last month, what would they say our top priority was?
x: Ian Hallett asks what happens to a decision between the moment it is made and the moment it is supposed to take effect.
The three handovers are from the leader to people three layers down, from the decision to a named owner with a date, and from the announcement to whoever controls time, people and money.

t: The Top Idea in Your Mind
q: I think most people have one top idea in their mind at any given time.
Which means it's a disaster to let the wrong idea become the top one in your mind.
The problem is that once you start raising money, raising money becomes the top idea in your mind.
You can't directly control where your thoughts drift. If you're controlling them, they're not drifting. But you can control them indirectly, by controlling what situations you let yourself get into.
These too are engaging in the wrong way: they have the same velcro-like shape as genuinely interesting ideas, but without the substance.
Someone who does you an injury hurts you twice: first by the injury itself, and second by taking up your time afterward thinking about it.
But it's easy to figure this out: just take a shower. What topic do your thoughts keep returning to?
x: Paul Graham argues that most people hold one "top idea" in their mind, the thought their attention drifts toward when allowed to wander, such as in the morning shower.
He says it is a disaster to let the wrong idea take that position, and illustrates it with startups that stall once they begin raising money.
He says it is a disaster to let the wrong idea take that position, and illustrates it with startups that stall once they begin raising money.

Since thoughts cannot be controlled directly, the practical lesson is to control the situations you let yourself get into, and to forgive injuries partly out of selfish interest in protecting your attention.
Disputes are the second major trap because they feel as engaging as real ideas but have no substance behind them.

t: The Slow Making of Dispositions
q: Bildung means the lifelong shaping of a whole person, in which knowledge, character and perception develop together.
Aristotle’s example is the experienced physician, who knows what to do for this patient, a knowledge that comes from many patients.
Murdoch’s claim is that the moral work took place in the looking, and that most of our ethical life happens in the quality of our attention before any choice arises.
The ballad describes a person who holds a powerful instrument without the formation that makes its use safe. Any technology that offers capability ahead of competence invites the same scene.
A trainee who never signs anything, never defends a choice to a sceptical colleague and never lives with an error has nothing for the inner spectator to build on.
The dispositions need practice, because they are habits. They need company, because mentors, colleagues and communities carry what cannot be written down.
A society that wants judgement, trust and accountability in its workforce will want to keep that soil rich.
x: Boymal starts from the Australian Treasury's 2026 Intergenerational Report, which says judgement, coordination, accountability, tacit knowledge and relationships will keep their value as AI automates tasks.

the teaching group outperformed the non-teaching group, with a more pronounced gap on the hardest questions on the test.

t: The Fastest Way to Lose Credibility With a New Leader
q: When a new leader arrives, most team members instinctively shift into impression-management mode. They highlight their significant accomplishments, position their skills, and look for opportunities to demonstrate their value.
Seasoned leaders have seen this before. They know that nearly everyone they meet in the first 100 days is auditioning. And because they know it, they discount it.
The team member who leads with their resume sparks skepticism, not confidence. The very behavior intended to build credibility erodes it.

The most credible thing a team member can do in the early days of a leadership transition is to identify what the organization really needs — even when that assessment is inconvenient for them personally.
They have put the organization before themselves. They have separated their recommendation from their fate. That is instantly and unmistakably credible.
Most people spend that window trying to look good. The ones who earn real trust spend it trying to be useful.
x: This Admired Leadership Field Note argues that team members who meet a new leader by promoting their own accomplishments damage the very credibility they want to build.
Leading with a resume in a leadership transition reads as auditioning, so new leaders discount it and the effort backfires.
This Admired Leadership Field Note argues that team members who meet a new leader by promoting their own accomplishments damage the very credibility they want to build.
The most credible move is to say what the organisation needs, even when the assessment is inconvenient for the speaker personally.
Separating a recommendation from one's own fate shows that the organisation comes before the person, which new leaders notice immediately.

t: The Detention Paradox
q: The problem wasn’t that sanctions didn’t work but that they only appeared to work for some students.

But using the behaviour of this group to judge whether detention deters students in general is like evaluating the effectiveness of speed cameras by only interviewing drivers who’ve been caught speeding. The most persistent offenders are, by definition, unrepresentative.
Experimental research on ‘third-party punishment’ has found that when people see someone punished for violating a norm, it changes their beliefs about what others approve of.

Keizer and colleagues called this the ‘spreading of disorder’ — a phenomenon all too common in schools. Observing violations, particularly those that go unsanctioned, reduces the likelihood of rules being followed in general.

There’s little reason to think that making a detention two hours long rather than one will somehow transform behaviour. Excessive or arbitrary punishment undermines the legitimacy on which effective discipline depends.
A rule which is repeatedly broken without consequence stops functioning as a rule. Students quickly learn what will be tolerated and adjust the behaviour accordingly.

So, here’s my conclusion: detentions only work for those kids who go with the flow. It would be obviously wrong to punish children who always behave well and kids who, like my younger self, always seem to do the wrong thing are unlikely to be persuaded by consequences they routinely fail to see coming.
x: Drawing on Atkins et al., Fluke et al. and experimental work on third-party punishment, he shows that sanctions seem to change behaviour for many students while failing for a persistent, highly aggressive minority.
Evaluating detention by the students who keep receiving it is a selection error, since the most persistent offenders are by definition unrepresentative of how sanctions affect everyone else.

Drawing on Atkins et al., Fluke et al. and experimental work on third-party punishment, he shows that sanctions seem to change behaviour for many students while failing for a persistent, highly aggressive minority.
Keizer and colleagues' graffiti experiments show disorder spreads, so unsanctioned violations lower compliance with unrelated rules across the whole school.

Certainty, proportionality and fairness matter more than severity, and a school should find something different for the student with the fiftieth detention rather than abandon the sanction for the other 49.
David Didau takes on the commonplace claim that detentions "don't work" because the pupils who collect the most of them keep misbehaving.
His conclusion is that detentions mainly work for the majority who go with the flow, because each enforced rule tells the whole community what the norms are.

t: Pick Up the Shovel
q: There’s a difference between working hard and working diligently. Working hard is about effort. Working diligently is about effort applied consistently toward something that matters.

Diligence is the willingness to keep doing the right work, even when the payoff isn’t immediate, because the work you do today isn’t just producing today’s result; it’s also producing the person you become in the process.
Covey wasn’t teaching his son how to mow a lawn. He was teaching him how to take responsibility for a result.
But if we’re always telling our kids exactly what to do, when to do it and how to do it, we can accidentally teach them that responsibility means following instructions.
And it’s not enough that they see you leave for the office. Your kids need to see you doing things around the house.
The important part is to let them own the work. Don’t hover. Don’t take over.
Because the greatest gift we can give our kids isn’t a life without difficult work. It’s the confidence to believe they can do difficult things.
x: He worked for cereal, for a hamburger and Coke, and for a paycheck, but the job that mattered most was a financial analyst role he did not enjoy and had to work hard to master.
Diligence is effort applied consistently toward something that matters, and the work done today also produces the person you become.
Covey's "green and clean" lawn shows that children learn responsibility when given ownership of a result, not a list of instructions.

Children watch what fathers do, so they need to see their dad doing the work that keeps the home running and finishing what he starts.

t: Opening the doors to a rich curriculum
q: Each component had good intentions behind it. Yet when leaders stepped back to look at the week as a whole, the reality was uncomfortable.
In trying to meet every specific need, these pupils had been handed a drastically reduced curriculum.

Learning was not organised around generic sensory exercises; it was anchored in subjects. Science, history, geography, art and music provided the context for communication, shared attention and curiosity.
The subject is not an extra hurdle. It is the vehicle through which development happens.
Transplanting a special school model wholesale was never going to work, nor was simply diluting standard lessons.
That bounded task was important because when teachers feel hesitant about teaching pupils with complex needs, it is rarely due to a lack of care. They are simply worried about getting it wrong.

Sitting in the same physical room as twenty-nine other children does not mean a pupil is included. A child can sit at the back with a teaching assistant and still be completely cut off from the subject.
We stop asking whether a child can manage the standard worksheet. We ask what the subject itself makes possible for them, and how we can open the door.
x: Well-intentioned specialist support can crowd out the wider curriculum, so leaders need to look at a pupil's whole week rather than each intervention in isolation.

Mary Myatt describes how the Compass Eko Trust, a group of twenty-eight schools across southern England, set out to build a genuinely rich curriculum for pupils with the most complex needs.
Mary Myatt describes how the Compass Eko Trust, a group of twenty-eight schools across southern England, set out to build a genuinely rich curriculum for pupils with the most complex needs.
Mapping the National Curriculum across three developmental profiles gave teachers a practical structure instead of a diluted version of standard lessons.
A bounded rollout, a single planning day and specialist colleagues alongside teachers dissolved mainstream teachers' fear of getting it wrong.
Real inclusion means meaningful participation in worthwhile knowledge, not simply being present in the classroom with a teaching assistant.
Myatt concludes that the starting question should shift from whether a child can manage the standard worksheet to what the subject makes possible for them.

t: On Hope
q: On a professional level, hope is simply not enough. I can’t hope the children in my school into getting good outcomes. I can’t hope for effective teaching.
In schools, hope may be the buoy on hard days but, my goodness, plans, precision, systems and - most importantly, people - are the enablers.
It takes graft - and in schools in challenging contexts a relentless, dogged, insistent graft over weeks and months and years - to sustainably improve.
It takes systems, the careful application of systems, the review of systems, and the chucking out of systems that simply don’t work.
At the risk of sounding pithy, it means keeping the main thing - what’s happening in classrooms, in front of kids - the main thing.
Leadership of schools in challenging contexts is unbelievably, unremittingly hard, and with societal shifts and erosion post-Covid, it has become harder.
x: Her answer is that hope is a buffer on hard days but never a strategy: children do not get good outcomes, teaching, behaviour, curriculum or attendance because someone hopes for them.
Stoneman separates hope as emotional buffer from the plans, precision, systems and people that actually produce results in schools.
Sustainable improvement in challenging contexts takes years of insistent graft rather than short bursts of inspiration.
Systems deserve regular review, and those that do not work should be discarded rather than defended.
She argues that leaders must ignore noise and keep what happens in classrooms the main thing, even as the buffets of leadership make that hard.
She names the toll of leading in challenging contexts, which has grown post-Covid, while insisting that difficulty is not an excuse.

t: On Being a Human
q: No human can be a means to an end. Every human must be the end for any other human.

You have taken an eternal thing, a human soul, and used that soul as a means to some selfish end. Achilles fractures the Greek army to get his prize back, and many die, including his friend Patroclus.
No man should treat women as “other,” because the totality of humanity is woman and man.
The thoughtful people in my life, including my mom, said, “Women are human first. Women are their own selves. Women are not ‘the other’ except to you.
At first, the Iliad seems like a “boy book,” but then any human realizes that the tragedy of the Iliad is men without women and women without voices.
Nobody does in the Iliad, though Hector comes closest in the love, genuine human love, he shows to Andromache. She is human to him, and so Hector is the most sympathetic.
Are men human? At the end of the Iliad, the answer is “no, not without women.
x: John Mark Reynolds reflects on how he first read Homer's Iliad badly, as a boy who wanted to look at Helen rather than honour her as a person, and how a slower graduate-school reading changed that.
He argues that Paris and Achilles both reduce a woman to a prize, which harms her and wrecks the Greek army, because a human soul can never be treated as a means to an end.
Treating a person as a prize to be won is presented as the common fault of Paris and Achilles, with damage that spreads from the woman to the whole community.
Reynolds concludes that men are not fully human without women.

t: Not Doing the Assignment Isn’t the Same as Not Learning
q: I take it the idea is that AI is your friend, the gym is homework or some educational activity, and building muscle is learning. So, if you have AI do your schoolwork for you, you aren’t going to learn anything.
It only follows that I didn’t go to the gym. It of course doesn’t follow that I didn’t do some other activity to build muscle!
Take me, as an example. Actually me. I never took your course. I never completed any of the assignments you believe are somehow essential, or at least helpful, for students.
I mean, honestly, how much immediate and long-term impact do we actually think we can have by spending 37.5 hours, over 15 weeks, at 10 a.m. on Tuesdays and Thursdays, with some random 18-year-old?

It is quite unclear to me why we think students have never had the opportunity to work with others—to plan, to push through conflict, to achieve something together—outside this course and this project.

If the goal is to support student learning around your discipline and students are not learning it through traditional assessment because they’re just having AI do it for them, then what other things might they do to benefit from their time in your course?
x: Dempsey takes aim at the popular argument that having AI do your homework is like sending a friend to the gym to lift weights for you.

His conclusion is a challenge to educators to ask what else students might do in a course that benefits them if traditional assessment no longer captures learning.

t: Knowing Your School
q: When we map territory we are interested in gaining a true and accurate picture. We set out with a range of tools, each designed to chart what we observe in particular ways.

Happiness and motivation cannot be whittled down to a number. Leaders could survey children to see how happy and motivated they are then aggregate this information and assign a percentage to it. But this aggregation wouldn’t be useful.
Fewer exclusions or suspensions over time is not necessarily symptomatic of improving behaviour. It could equally be that poor behaviour is now more tolerated.
Well, yes, but work in a book does not mean that the child still understands days, weeks or months down the line.

Standardised tests rarely measure what has actually been taught and although assigning a number like a standardised score might make it possible to compare performance to other children, it doesn’t tell us anything about whatchildren have or haven’t learned.
Again, the important bit is to get to the bottom of why colleagues feel as they do. Surveys won’t do that. Conversations will, but only if there is underlying trust.
Judgements are unreliable and unhelpful so visiting lessons in this way is simply to build shared understanding and look for ways to help childrento better understand.

Faced with such complexity and uncertainty, pragmatism is the order of the day. Leaders need to act quickly if it appears that children are unsafe or unhappy, but if school is calm and purposeful, we need not fall victim to the cargo cult fallacy of the usual monitoring activities.

Aggregated happiness or motivation percentages are not actionable; leaders learn more by knowing which individual children are struggling and then exploring why through conversation.

t: How to heal from overcommitment
q: Overcommitment works the same way. Everything you say yes to goes inside your backpack
Every yes is a decision. To make more intentional decisions you have to understand what drives them.
But we need to be honest: we’re not people pleasers, we’re self-pleasers. And it’s just human.
It’s a form of subconscious procrastination. You add things in your backpack to cover those hidden at the very bottom.
It’s not discipline, it’s not will-power, it’s just kindness. Towards myself. Because the correlation between overcommitment and burnout is simple
Don’t aim to be disciplined. Just be kind to yourself first.

t: How to Facilitate a Blameless Postmortem
q: The underlying belief of a blameless culture is that mistakes are generally a product of faulty organizational cultures rather than the fault of one or more individuals.
A blameless culture doesn't mean a lack of accountability. On the contrary, when teams own their mistakes, they learn from them, increasing ownership and responsibility.
In a just culture, people ask, "What went wrong?" versus "Who caused the problem?
Root causes are reasons at the optimal place in the chain of events where making a change would prevent the entire class of incidents.
Even if someone did something that directly led to an incident, instead of asking, "Why did (name) do this?" ask, "Why did the system allow/ encourage them to do this?
Quick wins can build momentum and remove unnecessary pain, while structural wins require more time and resources but will prevent costly and significant incidents from happening.
x: He defines a just culture as one that treats mistakes as products of faulty systems rather than individual failings, and notes this does not remove accountability.
Blameless does not mean unaccountable, because teams that own their mistakes together learn from them and take more responsibility.

Leaders should distinguish proximate from root causes and use the five whys to reach the point where one change prevents a whole class of incidents.
A blameless postmortem moves the question from who caused the problem to what went wrong and why the system allowed it.
His method has three steps: recap the event factually, reflect on behaviors and root causes using the five whys, and improve by choosing quick and structural wins with owners and deadlines.

t: How Easy is Grade 7 Unseen Poetry

t: Employee Data Use: One in Five Trust Leaders a Great Deal
q: One in five employees who work on a computer or another device regularly have “a great deal” of trust in their organization’s leaders to use employee data responsibly.

Forty percent of engaged employees have a great deal of trust in leaders to use employee data responsibly, compared with 13% of employees who are not engaged and just 4% of those who are actively disengaged.

They are more comfortable with constructive uses, such as supporting team effectiveness and development, than with uses that affect evaluations, staffing or scheduling.

t: Emergent Learning in Action: The After Action Review
q: One of the best sources of actionable knowledge is that which emerges from people’s own experience
Unlike post-mortems, the AAR is a continuing practice that is focused forward, generating lessons to be applied in the immediate future by the same people who developed them.
In a complex modern battlefield, the Army needed broadly skilled, thinking soldiers, not technicians with their faces in the rulebook.
We’re not opening 16 warehouses. We’re opening one warehouse 16 times.
The Army thinks learning has not occurred until an insight shapes actual behavior and is validated by results.
The first and best customers of a learning practice must be those directly involved.

t: Education Suddenly Changed, and I Didn't See It Coming
q: Since 2017 I’ve been protesting at the viral ability of social media to spread stupid ideas. It has savaged English teaching, where the two default teaching methods are now annotation and teaching paragraph structures.
After only 8 videos she has over 49,000 subscribers. That’s an outlier among outliers. In three months she has had nearly 800,000 views.

There are plenty of attacks against the cult-like approach to discipline at Michaela. But they are all philosphical. There are no exposes of teachers shouting and screaming at kids, because there is no shouting and screaming at kids.
Few of the attackers deal with the uncomfortable fact that every year Michaela’s students outperform every other secondary school in the country.

t: When Green Does Not Mean Good Growth
q: Weeds will take root when the growing conditions are unhealthy, and they can accelerate the decline of healthy growth. They can also disguise the underlying problems for a while.

But like the plush green lawn I thought I saw over the summer that was largely made up of weeds, our comprehension instruction that appears to be doing the job is simply not. Looking green and being healthy are not the same thing.

Foundational reading skills address a constrained set of knowledge and processes that students need to learn to be able to then perform them automatically. Comprehension is different. It is closer to thinking than to a set of discrete skills.

Even though there are components that can enable comprehension (e.g., fluency, vocabulary, syntax, anaphora, inferential reasoning), we can’t break down a reader’s understanding into discrete skills, teach those skills explicitly, and practice them until students can reliably produce correct answers.

t: Teaching on Purpose #18 No opt out
q: My hunch is that we probably don’t pay enough attention to precisely what we care about in the context of student understanding. This is something I explored with Christian on the podcast but in short, there is a trade-off to be made between breadth and depth.
Do we want to check the depth of understanding of a few pupils or even just one pupil… or is it more important that we check the headline understanding of the whole class?

The technique kicks in when you ask a student a question and they reply with ‘I don’t know’. At that point, the teacher asks another student before returning to the first student and asking them the same question again.
If they are able to compare the two responses from their classmates and decide which is the best, this tells the teacher that they probably do understand.

In this example, we have removed the barrier of the anxiety being triggered by being asked to articulate understanding publicly. But, we have preserved the key ingredient of the original technique – the requirement to articulate a depth of thinking.
The two incorrect answers are not chosen at random. They are chosen because of the likely misconceptions that are baked into them.
So, when it comes to Checking for understanding, as with all teaching decisions, even we are driven by the same purpose, it’s about doing the right thing at the right time for the right reason.

t: SIXTH REPORT: Alpha School’s Survival Challenge — literally
q: Alpha School put its students’ lives in danger during the Survival Challenge by confiscating their medical supplies.
What is known that is some of the medical supplies that students were deprived of over the weekend included epi-pens and inhalers, according to multiple sources.

What I have since learned through multiple sources is that Alpha School did not take the attendance of students once the Survival Challenge commenced — students were accounted for at the beginning of the event and when it concluded, but not in between.

This is why so-called normal schools take attendance with regularity: at all times, public schools must be able to account for the whereabouts of the children in their care in order to keep them safe.

t: Now That I Have Reiterated Your Opinion, Can You Summarize Mine?
q: Leaders first summarize the team member’s view and then request they return the favor by describing the leader’s opinion on the issue. In other words, they politely ask the team member to explain how the leader sees the issue.

t: Narrative Plenitude
q: Narrative plenitude is when so many stories are told about a particular cultural group that no single piece of media or art needs to carry the burden of defining that group.

t: From Sterilization to New Life: Vasectomy, Regret, and Reversal
q: Within the first six months of having the procedure, my wife and I were overcome with the sense that we had done something gravely wrong.
About 500,000 men get a vasectomy each year in the United States. By the age of 45, about 18% of American men will have had one.

Despite the relative ease of the procedure and the success rates, very few men end up having a reversal. Roughly 10% of those who have had a vasectomy return for a consultation to explore surgical options, and around 6% will ultimately have the reversal.
In contrast to the vasectomy procedure, which is considered medically necessary by most providers, there is almost no insurance coverage for vasectomy reversals.
During the ride home from the procedure with my family, the realization of what I had done really hit me: our family was open to life once more!

t: Your weekend was won… not given.
q: Hours worked by prime-age adults (everyone aged 20 to 59) have barely moved across the entire course of development. In the United States, prime-age hours were about 30 a week in 1900. They are about 30 a week today.
The point is narrower than that: a trade was made, over and over, and almost nobody decided to make it. There was never a moment where the choice was put to anyone.

t: The Equalizing Power of Friendship
q: Friendship is the term we use to describe the bond between two or more people which is, or has been, formed by a common interest, commitment, or love. C. S. Bans can block valuable uses, such as AI tools that give students far more writing practice and feedback than any teacher could deliver, and speech-recognition tools that target letter-sound gaps.
Regulating by whether AI is present is unworkable because AI is hard to define and is increasingly embedded in every kind of technology.
Policy should focus on the jobs a tool is doing (practice and feedback yes, spiritual counsel no) and on how well it does them.
Drawing on the history of electricity, she urges policymakers to act quickly on safety and privacy but to build a framework for watching real classroom use before regulating instruction.

The lesson: Don’t wait until temptation appears. Design your environment before it does.

The important question isn’t: “Can I get away with this once?” It’s: “What behavior am I reinforcing if I keep making this exception?
Good decision-making isn’t always about finding the option with zero downside. Sometimes it’s about choosing the option whose downside you can live with.
x: Odysseus has himself tied to the mast, which models making a binding system in advance rather than relying on willpower in the moment of temptation.
